items.body: A Vilnius-based Indonesian composer and a Berlin-based Japanese producer have recorded an album in three different nations and released it on an Ugandan imprint. As a result, Abu sounds as if it comes from nowhere and everywhere at once: a “mystifying new landmass, an imaginary island of ash.” To honor the spirit of the release, today’s review was born on one continent and the interview on another. Along the way, one will hear shavings of sound from each artist’s home. Johanes “Mo’ong” Santoso Pribadi and Shigeru Ishihara intermingle gamelan percussion and taiko rhythms with chants and shouts that seem to come from deepest Africa or from the heart of the volcano. The music imitates lava: erupting, flowing, burning and solidifying. Once it has disrupted the elements around it, Abu incorporates them into a new sonic landmass. In “Hai no uta,” two rings of an Indonesian bell preface more abrasive grinds and growls. A Javanese gong is struck; a high flute wails; a miniaturized choir sings a tiny song, recalling the Shobijin. The tension rises as the percussion begs to break through; and on “Abu,” it does. The tribal rhythms and guttural utterances recall KINACT’s Kinshasa in Action, also on Nyege Nyege Tapes; the continents seem connected again, honoring Pangea. The deep bass of “Palau” reflects subterranean rumble: while over too soon, it gives way to the even more enthralling “Wujud,” whose industrial stumbles and starts are melded to mechanical glissandos, an Orcan, deep earth factory. “Hino Tori” is a wild outlier, bursting forth with bangha rhtymns reminiscent of “Get Your Freak On” and swiftly adding a pounding techno beat; one can imagine this as a club killer on any continent. The metallic middle teases a far different audience before finishing a water bottle and plunging back in, even more energized than before. Those waiting for their thrash moment will find it on the chaotic, ensuing piece: a far cry from the Indonesian bells that launched the set only half an hour before. The LP’s primary draw, outside of its stunning juxtapositions of timbre, is its reaffirmation of a world without borders. Over countless millennia, magma has created innumerable landmasses, while the sea has often impassively reclaimed its own. Human borders mean nothing to geologic time. Abu is a reminder of the wealth of international music: entire species of music that much of the general public has yet to discover. We need not fear such encounters, as they do not threaten our own identity; quite the contrary. Instead, as in the case of Takkak Takkak, they broaden our language and deepen our experience. (Richard Allen) Takkak Takkak photo by @mr_guep Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi has kindly taken time out of Takkak Takkak’s touring schedule to answer a few questions about the production process for Abu. Your self-titled debut introduced a thrilling collision between DIY instrument building, Javanese traditions, Japanese electronics, noise, gabber and ritual percussion, often with a raw, playful sense of excess. On Abu, those same elements seem to have become part of a much broader imaginary world—less confrontational perhaps, but more immersive and narrative. Did you consciously set out to expand the language you established on the first album, and what did this fictional “island of ash” allow you to express that the debut could not? Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi: I don’t think we approached Abu by asking how to expand what we had done on the first album. It was more about continuing a conversation that had already started. By the time we began working on Abu, we had spent more time playing together, building trust and understanding how each other’s ideas and sounds could interact. Naturally, the music started to move into different directions. With the first album, we were discovering the chemistry between us. There was a lot of direct energy finding out what happens when handmade instruments, distorted electronics, ritual rhythms and dance music collide. Everything felt immediate and physical. For Abu, we had already developed a shared language, so we didn’t need to prove that those elements could coexist. Instead, we could ask where they might take us. The fictional island became a useful way of thinking because it isn’t Indonesia, Japan or anywhere else. It is a place where histories, myths, disasters and dreams can exist together without having to explain themselves. Ash is also an interesting material. It can represent destruction, but it is also what remains after transformation. New life often grows from volcanic ash. So Abu became less about representing a culture and more about imagining how things constantly disappear, mutate and re-emerge. One of the most fascinating aspects of Abu is the way it dissolves fixed notions of place and identity. The album was recorded across Yogyakarta, Švenčionėliai and Berlin, while drawing on Indonesian, Japanese and Baltic sonic environments without allowing any of them to dominate. Rather than presenting cultural traditions as fixed inheritances, the record seems to imagine them as constantly shifting landscapes. How did the experience of working across these different locations reshape your understanding of home, identity and collaboration? Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi: For me, identity has never been something fixed. Even traditional music is always changing. Every generation changes instruments, techniques and contexts. Tradition survives because people keep transforming it. Recording in Yogyakarta, Lithuania and Berlin reinforced that feeling. Each place has its own atmosphere, but we weren’t trying to collect local sounds like souvenirs. We were more interested in how our listening changed when we moved through different environments. Sometimes collaboration is less about combining different cultures than about creating a third space where nobody completely owns the result anymore. That’s what interests me. Instead of saying, “This is Indonesian,” or “This is Japanese,” we try to build a shared sonic ecology where those categories become less important than the relationships between sounds. In that sense, home is not only a geographical place. Home can also be a process of making things together. Your debut album was stylistically cohesive even with incursions into techno on tracks like “Salamander” and was driven by rhythm. One of the most striking aspects of Abu is its constant transformation and reflective nature. Ritual percussion gives way to hard dance rhythms, handmade instruments dissolve into electronic textures, and tracks such as “Api” and “Hino-Tori” move effortlessly between ceremony, ecstatic propulsion and the dance floor, while quieter moments like “Pulau”, “Nimbal” or “Funka suru mizu” provide spaces of suspension. Yet none of these shifts feels abrupt or arbitrary. How do you approach composition when working together? Do these transformations emerge intuitively through improvisation and experimentation, or is there an underlying architecture that allows such radically different musical languages to coexist so naturally? Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi: Our process is actually very fluid. We improvise a lot because that’s how we discover unexpected relationships between sounds. But improvisation is only the beginning. Afterwards we spend a lot of time listening, editing and thinking about how one sound transforms into another. We’re less interested in contrasting genres than in following the energy inside the sound itself. A ritual drum pattern and a gabber kick might seem completely different stylistically, but physically they both work on the body. They both produce collective movement, trance or repetition. Once you stop thinking in terms of genre and start thinking in terms of vibration, rhythm and texture, those transitions become quite natural. The quieter pieces are equally important because they allow the listener to breathe. Silence, space and suspension are also forms of rhythm. Without those moments, the more intense passages wouldn’t have the same impact. So there is structure, but it usually emerges after experimentation rather than before it. Both of your other projects—Raja Kirik (Johanes “Mo’ong” Santoso Pribadi with Yennu Ariendra) and Scotch Rolex (Shigeru Ishihara)—have always challenged musical categories, but Takkak Takkak seems driven as much by joy, humour and curiosity as by experimentation itself. In a musical landscape that often takes experimental music very seriously, especially within an ethnological framework, does playfulness become a creative strategy for opening listeners up to unfamiliar sounds and ways of listening? Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi: I think play is a very serious activity. When people hear the word “experimental,” they sometimes expect something difficult or intellectual. But curiosity usually begins with play. Children don’t separate learning from playing; they explore because they’re curious. I think music can work in the same way. Humour also helps remove fear. If listeners feel that they have to understand everything intellectually, they might close themselves off. But if they can laugh, dance or simply become curious, they’re already listening differently. In projects like Raja Kirik and Takkak Takkak, we’re interested in transformation rather than preservation. Traditional culture has always contained humour, absurdity, masks, tricksters and moments of chaos. Those aspects are just as important as the ceremonial or sacred ones. So playfulness isn’t there to make the work lighter. It’s another way of opening possibilities. Once people stop worrying about categories traditional versus contemporary, ritual versus club music, acoustic versus electronic they become more willing to experience sound on its own terms. (Interview by Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由立陶宛的印尼裔作曲家和柏林日籍制作人合作，在乌干达厂牌Nyege Nyege Tapes发行。甘美兰与太鼓节奏与非洲部落吟唱相互交织，音乐被比作熔岩的涌动——爆发、流动、凝固，再将周围元素吸收重组。印尼铃声、爪哇锣、高音笛声与工业噪音、机械滑音并存，某些段落如俱乐部打击乐般猛烈，另一些则呈现深沉的低频轰鸣。整张作品强调跨文化融合：大陆板块曾相连，音乐也应如此。两位艺术家跨越国界，在三种文化语境中录制专辑，证明了地理边界对真正的声音创造毫无约束力。评论还附带了采访内容，探讨了制作过程，为这张充满质感与张力的作品提供了创作背景。

items.body:
KAKUHAN / Sara Udon cellist Yuki Nakagawa takes a solemn yet dreamlike debut solo bow on the Unheard of Hope label - home to Mabe Fratti -  intently focussed on holistic examinations of his instrument, revealing its inner voices via various raw and processed strategies. RIYL Leila Bordreuil, Ecka Mordecai, Hildur Guðnadóttir, Okkyung Lee or Judith Hamann.

It's hard to explain just how eerily familiar Nakagawa's playing is, but you'll understand what we mean after hearing just a few moments of 'You Haze - I'. We've grown fully accustomed to the way Nakagawa handles the cello without even realizing it, absorbing his technique on records from KAKUHAN, his duo project with Koshihiro Hino, and Sara Udon alongside Naarm duo CS + Kreme. The way Nakagawa rests his bow between tones, picking up animated off-notes that make his sustained drones sound deep, dark and resonant, is genuinely personal, identifiable immediately. And although that aspect of his performance is front and center on his debut's opening track, it's the additional elements that tip us over the edge: the discreet, theremin-like wails that occupy a space just in the corner of the composition. 

After establishing his signature, Nakagawa veers away from his own convention sharply on 'CHU-MA', plucking the cello's strings and bending them as if they were attached to a koto. It's all remarkably stark at first, without much enhancement from Nakagawa's pedals and he slowly teases in different sounds that widen the instrument's range: woody creaks, knocks and growls that fill out its body and piercing overtones that go beyond the usual confines of the strings. Somehow, even using all these extended techniques, Nakagawa still manages to make music that's effortlessly enjoyable. It's bumpy, self-consciously experimental material, but not without roots - maybe best compared to Fred Frith's 'Guitar Solos' or Hans Reichel's 'The Death of the Rare Bird'.

There's even a prettiness to tracks like 'Upper and under the bridge' and 'You Haze - II' that betrays Nakagawa's resolve. But he's best when he's operating on the far fringe, turning his cello into a drum kit on the rickety, brilliant 'Grey test hits' or a vast resonator on the perplexingly huge 'Sange / Tsuki', an 8-minute xenharmonic spiral that sounds like an orchestra of fingerdrummed steel pans and a set of metal sheets being bowed in a concrete cavern. There's nothing else quite like it, we're sure of that.

items._cn_summary: 大提琴手Yuki Nakagawa首张个人专辑，以多种非常规演奏技法探索大提琴的声学可能性。作品融合弓弦延长技术、拨弦、共鸣器效应及电子处理，跨越多声律（xenharmonic）音律体系。曲目从'Grey test hits'将大提琴转化为打击乐器，到长达八分钟的'Sange / Tsuki'构建出如钢鼓与金属板在混凝土空间中共振的浩瀚音景。评论指出其风格可与Leila Bordreuil、Hildur Guðnadóttir、Ecka Mordecai等实验大提琴家比肩，演奏风格极具个人辨识度，根植于实验传统却形成独特语言。

items.body: With Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System, Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das abruptly change course from the expansive drone works of Meltwater Pulse (2023) and Dragon Rising (2022). The album arrives in violent bursts, assembled from Bangla rap, digital hardcore, dek bass, ambient electronics, and an unusually large network of collaborators stretching from Kolkata to Europe and East Asia. Its premise—a world descending into collective psychosis during the Kali Yuga, inspired in part by Das’s own experience of Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder—could easily have become an exercise in conceptual excess. Instead, organised chaos is built into the record itself. The constant collision of genres, collaborators, and production techniques refuses to settle into a single musical language. From the opening “Schizophrenic Intro”, the listener is thrown into a vortex of slowed-down, sped-up, looped, reversed, and glitched material, with no attempt to ease the transition. The abrasive momentum of “Gondho Jhaater Chule” barely relents in “Escape”, whose spectral vocals provide only the briefest moment of respite before “Iron Age Fantasies” introduces melodic gestures recalling classic Tollywood soundtracks, immediately distorting them into something deeply uncanny. “Laurar Baal” and “Laura Chos” push the collision between noise, Bengali rap, and sampled film dialogue to breaking point, while “E.M.P.” suspends the album inside an extended electronic blackout, one of its most absorbing passages. The unexpected arrival of the Korean gayageum and daegeum (the former a traditional twelve-string plucked zither with a wooden resonating chamber, the latter a large transverse bamboo flute known for its resonant, buzzing tone) on “Cappucc1n0” offers neither resolution nor sentimentality, but a fragile interruption before “Radio Paranoia” and “Maniac Outro” complete the descent into sonic disintegration. The use of crude sexual slang and bodily imagery—particularly in “Gondho Jhaater Chule”, “Laurar Baal”, and “Laura Chos”—adds another layer of instability, grounding the album’s apocalyptic vision in the language of the street as much as in mythology. Vulgarity and transcendence coexist throughout the record, collapsing distinctions between the sacred and the profane with the same ease that it moves between Bangla bass, digital hardcore, ambient electronics, and noise. The density of the album can feel overwhelming at times, and it continually rewires expectations. Yet every stylistic shift destabilises the previous one without feeling arbitrary, reflecting Das’s conception of schizophrenia not as a metaphor but as a lived condition in which disparate realities coexist simultaneously. The album’s many collaborators are given considerable freedom, yet the result never fragments into disconnected contributions; instead, their contrasting vocabularies reinforce the instability at the heart of the project. Challenging but consistently rewarding, Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System places the listener inside the eye of its own sonic vortex, where overload becomes its organising principle rather than an obstacle to it. Corresponding via email, Nilotpal Das sheds further light on the production process. photo by @roh4nlifts at Chandraketugarh Your earlier releases as Bios Contrast—from Dragon Rising and Meltwater Pulse to the forthcoming twelve-hour harmonium drone project under your own name—often revolved around expansive historical, geological, or spiritual concepts explored through long-form composition. Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System, by contrast, is fragmented, densely collaborative, and rooted in digital hardcore, Bangla rap, experimental electronics, and what you describe as “Brahmancore.” What drew you toward this radically different format? Do you see the album as a departure from your earlier practice, or simply another way of pursuing the same fascination with large-scale conceptual worlds? Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System is a very personal album. At the same time, it is a pursuit of a large-scale conceptual world. I wouldn’t say the theme of the album is conceptual, but rather very real. I suffer from Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder, so it’s a take on my worldview. Everything is random and unnecessary but, at the same time, needed, just like the world we live in. People would call me crazy, but I really felt the presence of something godlike, something that controls all of us humans. The album imagines a world descending into mass psychosis during the Kali Yuga, with schizophrenia functioning as both narrative device and sonic metaphor. At the same time, it brings together artists from very different musical and geographical backgrounds—BROOD, Kush Arora, Kim Hae Kyung, Ellery Everet, Seraphim, enesai, P.U.S.Y.E.T.E.R., and many others. How did you coordinate such a diverse group of collaborators while maintaining a coherent dramatic arc? Did each artist respond to a specific chapter in the narrative, or were they encouraged to reinterpret the concept through their own musical language? I didn’t make this album to express or present a very linear story. Every collaborator was free to interpret the concept in their own way. The record is schizophrenic in the sense that it collages many different sounds and genres while maintaining its central theme, which is chaos. And chaos happens naturally while collaborating. At first, I put out an open call for collaborators on Instagram. Many artists quickly DM’d me, and we started a group where we exchanged stems and sounds. Throughout your work you’ve often spoken about “curating sounds” rather than creating something entirely new, drawing on traditional instruments, field recordings, sampling, improvisation, and careful research. On Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System, that curatorial approach seems to expand into an entire network of voices, genres, and production methods, from Bangla rap and digital hardcore to ambient passages and Korean traditional instruments. Did working with so many collaborators change your understanding of authorship? At what point does a project of this scale stop feeling like an individual album and become a collective sound world? I started this project with the intention of creating the most mainstream, non-experimental trash music imaginable. The result, however, is the most experimental music I’ve worked on so far. I wasn’t controlling the direction the project was taking; it was a collaborative effort, and it still is. Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System is also the result of a video game that Kim Hae Kyung is currently developing, called The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System. In an earlier interview you described Kolkata as having only a small experimental music community, while also expressing admiration for artists working across South Asia. Since then, you’ve collaborated with musicians from Europe, North America, East Asia, and beyond, building an unusually international artistic network. Has making Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System changed your perspective on where your music belongs? Do you feel part of a global experimental community now, and how has continuing to work from Kolkata shaped the way you approach collaboration and the exchange of ideas? I would say I don’t belong to an experimental community anymore, but rather to a community that spans many genres, so I fit in with everyone. I like all kinds of music. Kolkata has always had a small experimental community, so I’ve simply accepted that and moved on to other communities. I like mainstream, hard-hitting music now—if the music goes hard, I’m all in, regardless of genre. I have a lot of connections with international artists, and I feel I belong to a global community rather than just a local one, because collaborating is fun, and collaborating with people who have totally different ideas and perspectives is even more fun. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: digital hardcore / experimental electronics / Bangla rap / noise / ambient
items._cn_summary: 这张作品以Kali Yuga（末法时代）集体精神崩溃为概念框架，将孟加拉说唱、数字硬核、dek bass、环境电子与噪声编织成一张高密度的拼贴。来自加尔各答至欧洲、东亚的多位合作者各自注入不同声响素材，加伽倻琴与大笒等东亚传统乐器以突兀方式介入，拒绝提供情感慰藉。专辑开篇即以变速、循环、反向与故障处理将听众抛入漩涡，粗糙的性俗语汇与神话题材并置，瓦解神圣与亵渎的界限。制作上刻意维持不稳定状态，每一风格转折都在瓦解前一段落，呼应创作者将精神分裂视为多重现实共存的生活体验而非隐喻。整体听感具有强烈暴力感与吞噬力，适合寻求极端实验融合的听众。

items._cn_summary: This Heat 1979年同名专辑被重新发行并经过母带重制。这张作品将流行、摇滚、先锋与电子音乐的边界彻底打破，被视为后朋克的源头之一。乐队在1970年代中期的布里克斯顿成立，由Charles Hayward、Charles Bullen、Gareth Williams三人组成。专辑融合多种实验手法，在磁带剪辑、磁带循环、反向录音等声音处理技术上极具开创性，影响了此后一代音乐人、制作人和录音师。乐评原文为该平台产品介绍式短评，文本较短，但所描述的音乐内容与用户的实验、先锋及暗潮后朋克口味高度契合，重制版由乐队自主厂牌发行。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以"暗影组曲"为概念，将室内乐编制融入前卫摇滚框架，形成独特的chamber prog风格。开篇以黑暗阴郁的室内乐序曲引入，随后曲目在主题变奏、节奏切换与情绪转换之间频繁游走，展现出极高的结构复杂度。大提琴、小提琴、巴松管、单簧管与钢琴、吉他之间形成丰富的对位织体，多种乐器组合的即兴互动成为作品核心驱动力。中段出现的中世纪风格短曲以及钢琴独奏段落，显示了作曲者对不同音乐传统的自如调用。专辑适合喜欢跨界融合与室内乐质感的听众，西班牙语标题与拉丁美洲文化背景为作品增添了独特的地域色彩。整体编排精致且充满探索性，但部分段落稍显冗长。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — ASCETA, the "ascetic ones" have emerged from their chamber prog hideaway somewhere in the the regionof the greater Santiago metroplex in Chile only to unleash their third lauded release THE FOOLLEADING THE BLIND which continues their uncanny ability to channel their inner Univers Zero, ArtZoyd, Rational Diet and other prerequisite classic chamber music oriented RIO acts that have keptthe musical underground electrified for the past half century. As an octet of classically trainedmusicians undergoing Cirque du Soleil musical acrobatics, this band weaves a conceptual tale offalse leadership through mass manipulation in an all-instrumental processions of classic avant-prog,chamber rock and avant-garde angularity. The album opens with the band's most energized and ambitious effort yet, the 21 1/2 minute titletrack which tackles the classic prog excesses in full dynamics. A versatile enigmatic excursionthrough a never-ending labyrinthine maze of motifs and crafty cadences, ASCETA goes for the progjugular right from the get go which continues the band's amazing display of instrumental interplaysounding like a seasoned symphony that has been in existence for decades but in actuality only amere six years in the making. With epic grandeur and bassoon-backed blazing bravado the title trackcatapults ASCETA to the top ranks of modern chamber prog, an exhilarating entryway to the band'sthird offering but also a bit of a false climatic start as it steals the thunder from the rest ofthe album's playlist.Although it swallows up nearly half of THE FOOL LEADING THE BLIND's playing time of 53 minutes, thetrack finally cedes to the following "Temple Of Mirrors" which offers a mesmerizing shorter arrayof twisted melodic constructs along with rock guitar grittiness and eccentric time signature changesrun amok, the quintessence of wily crazy complex prog along with dark and angsty atmospheres. "WhenThey Arrive" serves as the album's, uh ballad perhaps? A slow eerie and oozing instrumentalpowerhouse that remains true to the complexities of the album's true nature albeit with a touch ofmelancholic surrender. "Everything Stopped" on the other hand delivers a more bombastic introfollowed by a phantasmic slower procession of alternating instrumentation that has been compared toa cinematic score that offers an intensity that deserves some sort of visual counterpart. The albumends with the 10-minute closer "Momento Mori" which offers some of the strongest polyrhythms andavant-prog excess.Another strong album by one of South America's most dedicated chamber prog acts on par quality withthe greatest since the advent of the style's hybridizing effects that were spawned by the greatHenry Cow. An active album indeed as an inattentive listening session may result in jet lag howevercareful dedication to the procession of sounds that emerge will result in a most satisfying displayof modern avant-chamber prog in the finest of forms. If any complaints are to be made, i guess itfeels that ASCETA is very much going through the motions as traditionalists rather than offeringsome new stylistic rejuvenation and as mentioned, the title track seems to usurp the remainingalbum's intensity however despite a few nitpicking quirks that keep it from perfection, ASCETAcontinues to generate some of the most brilliant doses of this musical style since Rational Dietfolded in 2010. Add to that the entire concept thing seems a bit contrived as it seems like a progcheck list feature that really has no relevance to this music that seems to meander wherever itfeels. Nevertheless, amazing musicianship and captivating music.
items._cn_summary: ASCETA 来自智利圣地亚哥都市圈，是一支由八位古典训练出身的音乐家组成的前卫室内乐团。《The Fool Leading The Blind》作为他们的第三张专辑，以纯器乐形式呈现了一场关于虚假领导与大众操纵的概念叙事。专辑继承了 Univers Zero、Art Zoyd、Rational Diet 等经典 RIO/前卫室内乐的血脉，标题曲长达二十一分钟，以巴松管为核心驱动，展开密集的动机迷宫与复杂节奏对位，试图将交响乐般的厚重感压缩进室内编制。随后曲目节奏渐趋紧凑，扭曲的旋律构造与电吉他粗粝质感交织，缓慢段落则透出阴郁而压抑的氛围，尾声以多节奏叠加收束。整张专辑耗时六年打磨，展现出南美地区罕见的室内前卫深度，将古典语汇与摇滚能量熔于一炉。

items.body: Although Dirk Serries may have retired the Vidna Obmana moniker years ago, albums continue to be released under the name. While these are usually reissues or live recordings, this particular series is generating significant interest. The third installment in the “Twilight Of Perception Redux” series compiles rare and previously unreleased recordings from the Belgian project’s archives, spanning the years 1996 to 2006. The three CDs contain a total of 18 tracks, no fewer than 13 of which fall into the category of—let’s call them—‘curiosities’. Each disc features six tracks that immediately draw the listener into Vidna Obmana’s unique world. These are long, elaborate compositions characterized by generally slow, tribal rhythms that merge with deep, astral, and dreamlike soundscapes. Dirk Serries’ universe evokes a sense of mystery—and at times, a certain darkness—accentuated by field recordings and various forms of sound manipulation. At times, you feel as though you are wandering through a labyrinth of crystalline sounds; moments later, you are drawn towards an imaginary black hole, only to undergo an almost abyssal experience on the next track. Occasionally, a guitar emerges, played in an Ambient style that adds a touch of diversity to the overall atmosphere. Vidna Obmana was a project that fused different styles into a unique whole—a universe where Tribal and Ambient music formed a symbiotic relationship, sweeping the listener away into an imaginative world of richness, even on the darker tracks. This album is a perfect addition to the Vidna Obmana discography for many enthusiasts. Even decades after their creation, these tracks retain an irresistible allure—like a forbidden space where you simply have to discover what is unfolding inside. (Rating:8). Listen to “Threshold Of Obstruction”: Threshold Of Obstruction by Vidna Obmana About Vidna Obmana Vidna Obmana is the pseudonym of Belgian composer Dirk Serries, born in 1968. Serries recorded as Vidna Obmana from 1984 until 2007, when he officially retired the name, moving his active work to the Fear Falls Burning project. The name is Serbian for “optical illusion”. Working in Ambient, Minimal and Drone music, Serries released albums through labels including ND Records, Hypnos Recordings, Soleilmoon Recordings and Projekt Records, and collaborated with artists such as Steve Roach, Asmus Tietchens and Bass Communion. The original “Twilight Of Perception” appeared on Projekt in 1997. “Twilight Of Perception Redux Volume Three 1996 – 2006” compiles archival recordings from that period on Zoharum.
items._genre: dark ambient / tribal ambient / drone / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了比利时作曲家Dirk Serries以Vidna Obmana名义在1996至2006年间创作的稀见与未发表录音，共三张CD、18首曲目。作品以缓慢的部落节奏为骨架，与深邃空灵的音景相互交融，营造出神秘甚至略带黑暗的氛围。作者大量运用田野录音与多种声音处理手法，使听感在晶体般清澈的迷宫与近乎深渊的黑暗中反复切换；部分曲目中浮现的环境吉他演奏为整体氛围增添了层次。部落节奏与氛围音乐在此形成共生关系，将听众带入一个充满想象力的声场，即便在最暗沉的段落中仍保持着丰富的纹理。该系列作为档案性质的发掘，距原始创作已过去数十年，依然展现出持久的吸引力。

items.body:
Thee most coveted collection of Coil demos surfaces on CD, opening a window onto the recording sessions for their pivotal 1991 release, ‘Love’s Secret Domain’. 

Originally collated on a demo tape for WaxTrax! records in 1989 under the working title ‘The Side Effects of Life’, these are the raw early iterations of tracks that would become ‘Love’s Secret Domain’, and arguably one of the ’90s definitive albums. Only a handful of the original cassette are known to exist, and have understandably become important artefacts in their own right, so it’s a massive buzz to finally, physically grasp the album in its entirety, here supplemented by material off the ‘Wrong Eye/Scope’ 7”.

Between the album’s two bookending versions of ‘Fidgit’, which later appeared on the ‘WaxTrax! Sampler #2’ tape in 1989, the album spools familiar yet rawer examples of Coil classics such as ‘Dark River’, ‘Teenage Lightening’ and ‘Love's Secret Domain’, each replete with haphazard fades, cuts and stereo bias, and often with lots of ferric noise. However none of that should put prospective listeners off, with results more faithful to the original than the weirdly pitched version found on YouTube and p2p sites.   

Ultimately it’s a proper find for Coil diehards, but anyone intrigued by the hidden reverse of what was going on in parallel to Rave, grunge and post rock in the phase shift between later ‘80s and early ‘90s, should fill their boots.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了Coil于1989年为WaxTrax!唱片公司整理的演示磁带，原定名为《The Side Effects of Life》，是1991年关键专辑《Love's Secret Domain》前奏般的早期雏形。曲目以两版开场曲《Fidgit》框定整体结构，之间穿插《Dark River》《Teenage Lightening》《Love's Secret Domain》等日后成为Coil经典的作品的原始版本，保留了制作过程中的随意淡出、剪辑痕迹与立体声偏移，磁带底噪贯穿始终。相比流传于YouTube和P2P站点的变速版本，这些素材更忠实于原始录音。补充曲目来自《Wrong Eye/Scope》7寸单曲。整体呈现了八九十年代之交，在锐舞、垃圾摇滚和后摇滚并行发展之际，电子与工业音乐在实验边缘推进的脉络。

items.body:
One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interludes, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.
items._genre: ambient / analog synth / film score / hauntology / drone
items._cn_summary: Mark Jenkin以磁带质感的模拟合成器为笔触，描绘了一艘失踪拖网渔船多年后空船归港的康沃尔超自然故事。整张原声专辑脱离画面独立成立，音色处理成被海盐侵蚀的蓝灰色调，音墙如同铁锈与风化的青苔在礁石表面蔓延。海洋规模的持续低频嗡鸣与'海腿'般摇晃的循环段落交织，呈现出深刻的乡愁与失落感。AFX式的失真质感、BoC的朦胧片段感与经典民俗恐怖配乐氛围在此交汇，曲目之间的淡入淡出如鬼魂般的抖颤与失真贯穿始终。作品既是电影配乐，也是独立的氛围/暗潮音乐作品，适合在深夜独处时聆听。

items.body:
Weirder, wider, knottier and more hypnotic than its predecessors, L'rain's fourth album closes out her opening act with a vivid firework display of canny cultural references, considered observations and, most crucially, heartbreakingly beautiful songs. It's dumbfounding material, the kind of omnivorous, masterful gear that just doesn't come around often enough - a future classic, to put it bluntly, FFO keiyaA, Mabe Fratti, Dawuna, Dijon or even Broadcast.

There's an aura of comprehensiveness that surrounds 'fata morgana'. Taja Cheek has fully broken in her influences and inspirations at this stage and works without hesitation, painting out her experiences of a broken world with a level of insight that's so rare it's almost unparalleled. We already know that Cheek is a forensic listener; 2024's 'I Killed Your Dog' was a chunky "anti-break-up" album that met sorrow head-on with psych rock, indie, classic R&B and haunted folk references, while its predecessor projected Cheek's ambition, embedding shoegaze and ambient influences into a widescreen collage of avant-garde expressions. It wasn't fusion, exactly, it was Cheek's real-world experience - both as an artist and a high-profile curator - inked on thick, deluxe stock in illuminated letters. And the cycle that she began in 2017 with her tape saturated debut comes to a close with 'fata morgana'.

'I Killed Your Dog' was well aware of its lineage, recorded and produced with a level of detail that immediately put it alongside '70s avant-rock and R&B classics, so 'fata morgana' scratches away another layer, making deeper, odder connections. Even the brief 'rumors of light' is anything but throwaway, casually introducing Cheek's voice through a hailstorm of looped interference that's broken up by disarming bouts of silence. This doesn't only slickly establish the record's experimental credentials, it echoes the eerie 'Transmission' tracks on DJ Shadow's 'Endtroducing'. "This is not a dream," a garbled voice memorably stated, and Cheek's utterances hint at the exact opposite, a choppy mess of backmasked syllables, coughs and hesitations that suggest we're being lowered into a surreal fantasy. Fairytale muted piano phrases appear in the distance and 'with time' materializes on the horizon, kinked by buzzing oscillations that blur time just slightly until Cheek's whisper-sung vocals sidestep into the candlelight. 

Already, it's Cheek's most enigmatic track, occupying the confounding spot between an acid-tweaked Laurel Canyon memory, a half-heard gospel standard and Wendy Carlos's iconic 'The Shining' score: beautiful, meaningful and effortlessly cinematic. And Cheek continues to paint outside the lines, concocting half-song 'blue' from tape-mangled brass loops and gunky drum improvisations that she scrapes into a seductive, hazed atmosphere underneath her reverberating chorals. It's tempting to reference shoegaze or dream pop; the end result is similar, texturally at least, but 'fata morgana' is comprised of hardier raw material: minerals crushed by hand from funk, spiritual jazz, reggae, blues and rock 'n roll. That's never more obvious than on the gorgeous 'july 5th', when smudged folk - mixed with screaming feedback and analog bleeps, of course - mutates into a jerky soundsystem banger in its final act, imagining what OutKast's 'B.O.B.' might sound like if Atlanta was swapped out for Kingston.

Then there's the brassy standout 'elmyra', an anthemic start-stop post-pop banger that's part 'Haha Sound'-era Broadcast and part Wire, distorted to a level that would terrify most green-gilled pretenders. All this, and we haven't even mentioned the album's dense, maximalist lead single 'Soulless Cycle', a track that begins with chattering, bit-crushed samples and double-time kicks and lunges towards its glittering, psychedelic wall of sound that stands as an apt metaphor for the melancholy cacophony of contemporary reality. Before the album's done, Cheek slides in a lysergic slow jam ('birthday') and a near-ambient darkjazz diversion ('church of no one'), reminding us that perseverance and resilience is still possible - preferable, in fact.

Seriously, it's one of those albums that reminds you why you started caring about music in the first place, a milestone that's both cognizant of its place in history and hyper aware of the current moment. So, so good.

items._cn_summary: 这是L'Rain主创Taja Cheek的第四张专辑，被视为其创作周期的收官之作。乐评指出作品比前作更怪、更宽、更缠绕且更具催眠感，将心理摇滚、独立、经典R&B、鬼魅民谣、shoegaze与ambient等元素编织成一张充满文化指涉与个人洞察的拼贴。制作层面有大量磁带处理、loop干扰、反向人声与静音断裂，从DJ Shadow的拼贴美学到Wendy Carlos式的电影感配乐都有迹可循。歌曲在破碎的节奏与模糊的旋律中生长，钢琴短语与人声低语在混响中交替浮现，整体呈现出一种在酸民谣、半截福音与恐怖片配乐之间漂浮的奇异氛围。乐评将其定位为一张罕见的、跨类型且高度个人化的当代专辑，对喜欢实验拼贴与avant-pop的听众具有很强吸引力。

items.body:
In the 15+ years that have elapsed since 'Loop Finding Jazz Records' first shuffled out of his ambrosially dusty speakers, Jan Jelinek's most famous album has acquired an almost mythical status. Originally released via Pole's defunct Scape imprint, it now finds new life via Jelinek's own Faitiche label, for a new generation to marvel at one of the finest examples of loop-based electronic music typical of the early noughties.

Taking what reads like a pretty austere set of ingredients, Jelinek's technique revolves around a trio of elements which consist of second long cuts of 1960's-70's jazz recordings, the loop-finding modulation wheel (do your homework!) and the Moiré effect; albeit rendered in the acoustic as opposed to the image and spectral domains.

If all this sounds a bit academic, be assured that on record it is anything but; as crumbling edifices of mealy rhythms slowly pulse into life and swirl around your head like snow storms clashing with a dust devil. Taking sediments of fathom deep static then skimming the best stuff from the top, Jelinek opens through the dampened echoes of 'Moiré (piano & organ)' wherein a slow-motion thrum of spiraling clicks, rustles and analogue tones conspire to give the impression of recondite perspectives that extend well beyond the constituent elements.

Elsewhere, 'Rocky in the Video Age' instills a gratuitously optimistic blush to the aquatic micro-sound ebb, 'Moiré (Strings)' is a perfect companion to Basinski's disintegrating tape archive, whilst 'Them, Their' represents an aural crease so sleight you can only catch its distinctive gleam from the corner of your eye.
items._cn_summary: Jan Jelinek 1999年的经典专辑以极简手法处理爵士素材：将六七十年代爵士唱片切成秒级碎片，借助Loop Finding调制轮与声学领域的莫尔效应，让微小的声音颗粒在循环中互相干涉叠加，形成缓慢脉动的纹理。评论将这种学术化的采样与重组描述为尘土飞扬的雪暴与微声的漩涡，每轨呈现不同侧面——《Moiré (piano & organ)》以潮湿回响展开深景，《Rocky in the Video Age》注入一丝乐观光泽，《Moiré (Strings)》与Basinski的磁带衰败档案遥相呼应，《Them, Their》则是几乎不可捕捉的听觉折痕。这张作品在采样艺术领域具有标杆地位，由Jelinek自己的Faitiche厂牌再版，让新一代听众得以重新进入这片声音考古的沉积层。

items.body:
One of the most influential, insular and multi-layered albums of the last five decades, created through endless hours of improvisation - involving almost fifty musicians and recorded in complete darkness, 'Spirit Of Eden' was a radical departure for Talk Talk, ' an album that has attained almost mythical status since its release in 1988.

Following the commercial success of their singles "It's My Life", "Life's What You Make It” and album "The Colour of Spring”, Talk Talk retreated into the shadows and produced an album that still defies categorisation. Mark Hollis is said to have demanded the players record in almost complete darkness, improvising for hours to produce individual parts without hearing any backing tracks or surrounding material.

"Spirit Of Eden" is one of the most fearless and rewarding leaps a commercially successful band has ever taken, and continues to cast its influence almost 40 years later.
items._genre: experimental / post-rock / improvisation / art rock / ambient
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Talk Talk在商业成功后的一次彻底转向，近五十位乐手参与，通过长时间即兴录制完成，制作过程中演奏者在近乎全黑的环境下各自贡献片段，彼此听不到其他音轨，最终拼合为一张层次极为丰富的作品。整张专辑拒绝归入任何已有类型框架，既保留了乐队前作中旋律化的敏感性，又将大量空间感、环境声与缓慢展开的结构融入其中。从编曲角度看，它将管弦乐元素、爵士即兴、民谣质感和原声吉他并置，形成了极为罕见的混合美学，对后世众多实验与后摇乐队产生了持续影响。作为180克半速刻盘再版，强调了原始录音中那些细微的动态与空间细节，对于关注实验与即兴传统的听众而言，这是一张值得反复聆听、不断从中发现新层次的作品。

items.body:
Stefan Betke aka Pole’s hugely influential debut LP of frayed dub experiments resurfaces for a 20th anniversary reissue, taking us back to smoked out nights at the turn of the century and some of the finest post basic-channel dub echoes ever released. Essential listening if you’re into anything from Rhythm & Sound to Vainqueur, Jon Hassell to Jackie Mittoo.

As legend goes, Pole took his name from a malfunctioning Waldorf 4-Pole filter which produced hisses and pops which weren’t really controllable or predictable, much like a living organism. Betke realised the potential and came to alchemically morph and render them with judicious FX dubbing into a groundbreaking sort of minimalist electro-dub that sounds exceedingly good with a spliff and glass of booze. Working somewhere between the variants of abstract techno on Chain Reaction and Mille Plateaux’s cutting edge minimalist strains, Pole’s first trio of albums inarguably helped lay the foundations for dub techno as it’s come to be known and are held in the highest regard by practically everyone who owns them. 

The Pole aesthetic is patently laid out in ‘1’, where his organic clicks ’n pops come out to play accompanied by lilting organ and jazzy bass channelling Jackie Mittoo via Jon Hassell and Rhythm & Sound into a uniquely, gauzy, gaseous state.  So strong was the impact of the album on the late ‘90s underground, they even generated a “pastiche” that was unwittingly issued (and subsequently deleted) by Fat Cat on their split series, but was purportedly made by V/Vm in a snidey but frankly hilarious prank, albeit one that demonstrates just how ubiquitous and influential Betke’s sound was at the time. More than that, it’s fair to say the 20 year cycle hasn’t rinsed out the appeal of this triptych one bit; it remains one of electronic music’s most enigmatic and strangely moving, tactile bodies of work.

items._cn_summary: Pole首张专辑发行20周年再版。Stefan Betke利用损坏的Waldorf四极滤波器产生的不可控噪音与爆裂声，通过精妙的混响效果将其转化为极简电声dub。专辑介于Chain Reaction的抽象techno与Mille Plateaux的前沿极简之间，奠定了dub techno这一类型的美学基础。有机click声与管风琴、放克贝斯线交织，形成独特的朦胧气体般质感。专辑影响深远，曾有V/Vm的恶搞戏仿作品在Fat Cat厂牌发行后被召回，足以证明其声音在当时的无处不在。二十年后再听，这套三连作仍保持着电子音乐中最神秘、感人而具触感的艺术生命力。

items.body:
Picking up where 2024's 'Trash Can Lamb' left off, Keith Freund blurs the line between acoustic instrumentation and DIY electronics on his latest full-length, unraveling his gentle, jazzy sessions with 8-bit beats and oddball FX.

Since the beginning, Freund has been fixated on the character of a sound rather than what that sound, on its own, might represent. His piano parts rarely come off as if they've been played by hand; after chopping them to shreds, he inevitably reconstitutes them into player-piano style impossible sequences, re-organizing the notes and re-sculpting the tone completely. On 'Over Sidewalk Bryum', for example, it's the piano that provides the track's rhythm, accented by radio interference and bit-crushed oscillations. And although Freund does less chipping at his horn parts, letting the sax soar over the chattering electronics, it's still subtly tweaked - nothing's ever quite what it seems.

A swamp of discarded blips and glitches help prop up 'I'll Find a Place for Us', and Freund's soft woodwind tones make their way through the noise initially - or at least that's what we're supposed to think. In time, Freund's sax emerges and the soft-hued, woodwind-like sound is revealed to be a red herring. But that's the kind of sleight of hand that Freund seems to revel in, creating glitchy, unstable music from soft, placid sound sources, not the harsh digital detritus you'd expect to find on a Mille Plateaux disc.

items._cn_summary: Keith Freund延续了2024年《Trash Can Lamb》的探索方向，在原声器乐演奏与自制电子设备之间进一步模糊边界。他将爵士钢琴拆解重组为自动钢琴式的不可能音序，重新编排音符、彻底重塑音色，使钢琴听来几乎不像人为演奏。萨克斯段落虽较少经过切碎处理，却仍被微妙调整，漂浮于电子碎屑之上。在《Over Sidewalk Bryum》中，钢琴提供节奏骨架，搭配无线电干扰和比特压缩振荡；《I'll Find a Place for Us》则以废弃的故障杂音搭建底噪，柔和的木管音色先隐后显，构成听觉骗局。整体而言，Freund从柔和宁静的声源中制造出不稳定、故障化的音乐，与典型的工业电子厂牌作品形成鲜明区隔，展现出个人化的声学逻辑与声音戏法。

items.body: This, unfortunately, digital only release is a treat, a future hidden gem, probably, for all those interested in the free thinking ethos of improvisation. Jack Wright is on the saxophones (alto and soprano, I believe) and Bennett on the drums and some other percussive objects. Tourne is comprised of three long tracks, each over or around the ten minute mark, and presents their take of playing live. When I’m saying that this is their take, I mean it literally. Even though there’s a certain generational gap when it comes to those two players’ age, they both refer to the early days of free improvisation (we could comment that those days where having jazz as a reference but nothing more) when a new language –every sound is possible and only the players are liable for it- was being formed and presented through playing live. This is how both of them antagonize with their preconceived ideas about playing music: by challenging each other to go further and further, even beyond the margins of what is sound, what is music, what is that should be heard from percussion and saxophones. This is not their first collaboration but, still, they sound fresh and willing not to fall in the shaky ground of presenting “good” music-not even playing “challenging” and “adventurous” stuff. They just are themselves, staying true to the basic ethos of free improvisation. Trying, at least, to present something new each time. Bennett’s playing is agile, feverish and energetic as never before. He seems to be enjoying himself as he releases low level percussive barrages. Wright, restless as ever, follows but also runs in parallel releasing saxophone sounds as if his respected instrument is made of rubber and can bend and displace notes and phrases. I’m not sure if I made my point clear out to you, but this is a joy to experience release that has to be, at least, listened by a lot of people. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由萨克斯手Jack Wright与鼓手Ben Bennett合作，仅以数字形式发行，包含三首时长约十分钟左右的即兴作品。两人虽存在年龄代际差异，但共同回归自由即兴的早期精神——一切声音皆为可能，玩乐者全权负责。他们在现场中互相挑战，不断突破声音与音乐的边界，甚至超越萨克斯与打击乐的传统定义。Bennett的演奏灵活而狂热，以低强度的打击轰炸释放能量；Wright则不安分地让萨克斯发声如橡胶般弯曲变形，扭曲音符与乐句。专辑不追求所谓的好音乐，也不刻意标榜冒险性，只是忠实于自由即兴的基本精神，每次尝试呈现新东西。这种纯粹的即兴态度与对声音本质的持续探索，使其成为该领域值得关注的一次录音。

items.body: Based in Gothenburg, SYNVILLA treats music and moving images as organs within the same unruly body. Heavy experimental rock, psychedelia, post-punk, and noise meet video art that is seductive, threatening, and frequently difficult to separate from the performance itself. Riffs drag and buckle, rhythms take crooked routes, and warped melodies push through distortion with a streak of playful menace. During their live performances, SYNVILLA uses projected video as part of the stage presentation. While the band plays, footage of bodies and faces repeats, divides, and distorts across the screen, changing in step with the music. The projections give the audience a visual extension of the songs and place video art at the center of the concert experience. SYNVILLA return with their latest single, Milky Breath, released through Beans on Toast Records. The song accompanies the announcement of the forthcoming GRINDMOTHER EP. Thick drums give Milky Breath a heavy, deliberate gait. Psychedelic guitars slither around them in warped curves, while a buzzing low register carries the chest-deep vibration of a didgeridoo. Above this mass, the vocals quiver with witchy poise, stretching each phrase somewhere between a warning, an invitation, and an involuntary exhalation. The arrangement gains force through repetition as its parts return slightly damaged, bend out of shape, and eventually break into a physical act of release. SYNVILLA describes the song as a surrender of conscious control, with social masks falling away as bodily impulse assumes command. The title intensifies that tension: milk suggests nourishment and breath signals life, yet the two words together feel thick, close, and almost claustrophobic. Resistance registers as muscle memory, the body shaking loose the instructions it has learned to obey. Few smiles in recent memory have looked as hungry as the one occupying the Milky Breath video. A black-clad figure appears beneath two enormous horn-like forms while its mouth stretches into a crowded, impossible crescent, recalling the Mouth of Sauron in Peter Jackson’s The Return of the King. The eyes vanish, the head divides, and the grin remains fixed, as though it has taken possession of the person wearing it. Victor Cornelius turns that premise into five and a half minutes of analog-video mutation. Solarized pinks, acidic orange, and cyan pass over faces and anatomical forms. The central figure is duplicated into contact sheets, folded into bilateral symmetry, pressed behind mesh, and expanded into a featureless white oval. Banks of lidless eyes crowd the frame while faces swim beneath watery tracking errors, hands skitter across a doubled torso, and human figures collapse into stark silhouettes. Throughout these transformations, the enormous grin functions as a gruesome visual refrain. It survives every attempt to erase the face around it, repeatedly returning with its wet rows of teeth intact. By the final passage, the video resembles a late-night television transmission seized by an intelligence that has only recently learned the mechanics of a human smile. Watch the video for Milky Breath below: With two albums behind them, SYNVILLA celebrated their latest release, Feberfoster, with a sold-out concert at Skeppet GBG. The collective has shared stages with Hällas, Skraeckoedlan, and MaidaVale, while appearing at festivals including Fuzztival, Muskelrock, and Sonic Ritual. Milky Breath is out now through Beans on Toast Records. The forthcoming GRINDMOTHER EP will follow, with its release date to be announced. items._cn_summary: 瑞典哥德堡实验集体 SYNVILLA 将音乐与动态影像视为同一有机体的器官，重型实验摇滚、迷幻、后朋克与噪音在扭曲的旋律与沉重的鼓击中交织，低频嗡鸣如迪吉里杜管般震颤胸腔，人声在警告与邀请之间摇摆不定。最新单曲《Milky Breath》以重复构建力量，部件逐渐变形、断裂，化为身体性的释放，乐队将这种失控描述为社会面具脱落、身体冲动接管意识的屈服。与之配套的影像由 Victor Cornelius 执导，五分半钟的模拟视频中，极端视觉处理——日光化色调、对称分割、网格叠印与追踪失真——将人物面部反复拆解，而那张贪婪的咧嘴笑容始终顽固存续，构成贯穿始终的恐怖视觉副歌。整件作品模糊了现场表演与影像艺术的界限，将视频艺术置于音乐会体验的中心，是一次声音与画面互为延伸的实验性实践。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是葡萄牙先锋音乐人 Rafael Toral 在 Jim O'Rourke 传奇厂牌 Moikai 二十多年来首次发行的作品。整张专辑以极其缓慢的速度展开，将爵士启发的吉他音乐拉长为接近凝固的绵延状态。他使用自制合成器模仿鸟鸣，与拉伸的钢弦持续低音相互交织，营造出微妙的管弦乐质感。在作品中可以看到对 Bach 和声逻辑、Loren Connors 极简吉他美学、Gavin Bryars 的低沉质感以及 Rhys Chatham 的长篇结构美学的综合回应。传统和弦进程依然存在，但被以炼金术般的技法重新排列与延伸，模糊了即兴与作曲之间的界限。专辑以长篇作品形式呈现，强调时间的感知与声音细节的微观变化，是当代实验音乐场景中具有标志性意义的作品。

items.body: Bassist Alexander Frangenheim and saxophonist Stefan Keune belong to the third generation of European Improvised Music (or fourth, depending on how you calculate). I came across Keune and his trio with bassist Hans Schneider and drummer Achim Krämer with No Comment (FMP 2009), Frangenheim was on my radar because he was a member of Cecil Taylor’s Workshop Band ( Legba Crossing , FMP 1988) and later on he released several very good recordings on the Creative Sources label. Their musical style - not atypical for European Improv in the 1990s and 2000s - was more abstract than the recordings of the godfathers of this music which - while experimental - were often very concrete. Whereas concrete improvisation works with direct, tangible materials, situations, or predetermined rules - be they small melodies, energetic structures, or even a pure desire for destruction (one need only think of Peter Kowald’s and Peter Brötzmann’s “Kaputtspiel” phase - even if the latter disliked the term), abstract improvisation detaches itself from external circumstances to express feelings or states of mind primarily through sound, structure, and form. Abstractions are evident in many ways on New Traces , Frangenheim’s and Keune’s debut collaboration as a duo: first, in the pauses - moments of silence that are repeatedly interspersed among the music’s hectic passages, as in “New Traces 1” or “New Traces 7” - and second, in the music’s extreme density and concentration. Both musicians employ extended playing techniques such as harmonics, overtones, and percussive strokes. It’s not about melodies, but about exploring timbres, textures, and dynamic extremes. Ultimately, however, the abstract moments are most evident in the frenzied runs and competing trills, the contrasts in register (especially in “New Traces 4“, where they really reach the limit of what listeners can bear to hear), the impetuous stylistic drive, and the simultaneous clarity of the sound. True, Keune still hisses, coos, hums, and gurgles for all he’s worth, and Frangenheim scrubs away, making his bass weep and crash - yet it’s as if one had stripped Barry Guy & Mats Gustafsson’s Sinners, Rather Than Saints (No Business, 2009) of all its embellishments, oriental flourishes, vibratos, frills and obvious crescendos (don’t get me wrong, I love this album) - to draw a concrete example for comparison. Just listen to “New Traces 8“. Here, the improvisation takes unpredictable turns and surprising sounds are created, yet the structure of the piece remains crystal clear. A prerequisite for this is that both musicians have such an excellent technique that during the more frenzied moments, instrumental timbres coalesce without getting in one’s way. The album is a treat for fans of abstract music and sonic exploration. Very recommended. New Traces is available as a download. new traces by Frangenheim / Keune Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 贝斯手Alexander Frangenheim与萨克斯演奏家Stefan Keune合作的二重奏专辑收录了多首以编号命名的即兴段落，被归入欧洲即兴音乐第三或第四代传承者的脉络。乐评将欧洲九十至两千年代盛行的抽象即兴与前辈的具体即兴做了对比，指出本专辑的核心特征在于声音质材、力度极限与结构形式的抽象表达，而非旋律或预设规则。两位乐手大量运用泛音、泛列与打击性技法，在密集狂热的乐句与突然的静默之间频繁切换。专辑强调演奏者需具备的高度技术控制力，使乐器音色在激烈段落中既融合又彼此独立，是一张面向抽象音乐与声音探索爱好者的作品，以数字下载形式发行。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.

items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 联合作曲家 Paladino 与诗人 Ferrari 推出专辑《Songs of Compassion》，共十一首曲目。音乐以钢琴为核心，佐以弦乐、木管、合成器铺陈与金属感音色，旋律不以传统功能和声推进，借鉴极简主义脉络，介于氛围与调式之间。Moskowitz 的演唱将文本置于首位，旋律随意识流起伏，钢琴有时充当评论的希腊合唱。歌词直面当代政治议题，如《Pale Wanderer》警示威权主义的共谋结构，《Charlottesville》直接引用游行者口号，延续六十年代抗议传统并融入对死亡与宇宙位置的沉思。整体在声学实验与社会书写之间取得平衡，挑战听者对西方和声逻辑的固有认知。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

Beneath the often abrasive drums, and the chugging guitars that feel ripped out of both nu and industrial metal, there’s something tender that’s trying to reach out from the depths and break through. items._cn_summary: 牛津郡独立艺术家 He Didnt 带来专辑《Dark Making》，以暴力的工业嗡鸣为外壳，却试图在深处呈现某种柔软的情感张力。专辑由尖锐的鼓击与循环失真吉他 riff 驱动，开篇曲《Bass Tape Loop》以断奏扫弦与反馈噪音撕开序幕，单音合成器在底层持续延展，逐步将粗糙声响转化为层次丰富的音景。整张作品在工业金属的猛攻与传统嗡鸣结构的绵延之间游走，既有实验声响的侵略性，又保留了情绪上的克制与留白。这种刚硬表层下的脆弱表达，构成作品核心的聆听价值。

items._cn_summary: ASCETA首张全长专辑以一首二十余分钟的标题曲展开，呈现了密集的构思与未完成的谜题感，后续短曲逐步收紧结构。第二首以巴松与大提琴的对位线条为核心，动态更为凝聚；第三首以钢琴和弦乐铺垫缓慢开场，主题经历变形后回归首尾呼应的形式逻辑；第四首被乐评视为全专辑最完整的作品，巴松主导的张力构建与旋律主题层层堆叠；末曲在动态引子后迅速切入受控的混沌，频繁转调与骤停交替，终结于意料之外的尾声。整体延续了RIO与前 Prog的语法，在古典室内乐编制中注入实验性结构逻辑，对偏爱前卫融合的听众具有较高探索价值。

items.body: Any album that sounds as though everybody involved remembered to wipe their feet before entering the studio should probably be regarded with suspicion. Fortunately, Wailin Storms’ The Arsonist sounds more like four people discovered a door already hanging crooked from its hinges and decided the sensible course was to make the room less structurally sound. The Durham band carries the American South around like a family curse, hauling blues, gothic rock, punk, doom, Baptist hymns and old folk dread into the same cramped quarters. Their fifth album, and first for Season of Mist, was recorded fully analogue by Matt Talbott of Hum, an appropriate choice for music that benefits from scraped edges and human error. Justin Storms wanted portions of the record to reconnect with the primitive four-track character of the band’s beginnings. “Some of these songs are more primitive and stripped down, hearkening back to the four-track recordings that the band started with,” says Storms. “The recordings contain flaws, but remain human in all the right ways. They could be a murder ballad or an old folk song that’s sung around the campfire.” Standout track Dead End provides an appropriately diseased introduction. Ben Melton’s guitar worries at Steve Stanczyk’s bass while Mark Oates pounds out a rhythm that seems increasingly annoyed about being alive. There is some Radiohead in its queasy grandeur, the poetic ecstasy of The Doors’ Jim Morrison, and plenty of The Gun Club in its bloodshot blues logic. Then Storms sings “Calm night / Birds keep plucking out our eyes” with the casual authority of a man reporting local traffic conditions. Fire has followed Storms since childhood, when his fascination with flames nearly resulted in the destruction of his family home. Here it becomes appetite, catastrophe, sex, faith and bad judgment sharing one cigarette. Flannery O’Connor would recognize the neighborhood immediately: everybody has dressed for church, salvation is theoretically available, and somebody somewhere has misplaced a can of gasoline. You Never Answered turns the miserable modern habit of staring into a phone into a deafening plea for actual contact. Elsewhere, war and ordinary social machinery feed the record’s agitation before the title track slows everything into a bruised procession. Love suddenly becomes another uncontrollable force capable of rearranging a life without requesting permission. Never Rest swells into a crescendo of horror as it unfurls a wild torrent of haunting poetry set against apocalyptic guitars and thundering drums – landing somewhere between Type O Negative and The Doors. The Arsonist finds Wailin Storms standing dangerously close to their oldest impulses: primitive rock & roll, folk horror, damaged romance and the suspicion that salvation and catastrophe may share an address. items._cn_summary: Wailin Storms 的第五张专辑《The Arsonist》由 Hum 的 Matt Talbott 操刀全模拟录音，刻意保留磁带瑕疵与原始质感，将布鲁斯、哥特摇滚、朋克、厄运金属与浸信会赞美诗压缩进同一空间。主脑 Justin Storms 明确希望回归乐队早期四轨录音的粗粝与原始，使这些歌曲既像古老的谋杀民谣，也像篝火旁传唱的民间歌谣。乐队成员 Ben Melton 的吉他缠绕 Steve Stanczyk 的贝斯，Mark Oates 的鼓点带有一种对存在本身的厌倦感。《Dead End》将 Radiohead 的不安壮丽、Jim Morrison 的诗意迷醉与 Gun Club 的血红布鲁斯逻辑熔于一炉。专辑核心意象——火焰、灾难、信仰与败坏的浪漫——让 Flannery O'Connor 式美国南方哥特叙事贯穿始终。

Unlike his recent output centered around extended, hypnotic compositions, the fourteen tracks here immediately reques
items.body:
Lower case, gently effervescent electronica from the softer underbelly of the US scene, turning extramusical cues from the collected writings of Julian of Norwich - the earliest writing of any woman in English.

“On revelations of divine love, jason calhoun’s fifth release for Dear Life Records, Calhoun has assembled an especially potent album of work that whirrs, hums, and glows. Unlike his recent output centered around extended, hypnotic compositions, the fourteen tracks here immediately request your attention and curiosity. Their concision only underscores one of his greatest strengths: the ability to capture an evaporating, fleeting moment, and hold it close.

The title is a nod to British Anchoress Julian of Norwich, whose collected writing of the same title is the earliest of any woman written in English. Here it serves as a unifying theme for Calhoun's particular palette of restless textures and tentative melodies. This is personal music, to be sure, but it also feels tactile, almost taffy-like in its presentation—and with such a potent combination, it is hard to resist a smile while listening. Like when the insistent pulse grounding 'last one' suddenly changes color as yawning tones reveal themselves, or how 'eye dilation' tiptoes into the room with each note sounding like a carefully chosen step. Though never precious or fussy, the album remains resolutely intimate.

Calhoun puts it plainly: “Julian of Norwich says “‘All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well’. These days, I’ve been having my doubts that this is true. As no solution to the issue at hand, I look for the revelations of divine love in my life, and I find them--in my partner asleep on the floor in our studio, my survival of a social interaction with a stranger, being bad at chess. Don't ask me what they mean-I'm still figuring that out myself. Maybe we can figure it out together.” It is from this place of doubt, searching, and openness that the album finds its footing.

When asked about the origin of the album's cover art, Calhoun explained, "I see this spot all the time on my commute home from work". A true statement of how the mundane and meaningful are interwoven, from someone who celebrates that union better than most. Unlike Julian of Norwich, Calhoun is no hermetic mystic himself-but in his daily life he works at an oncology center, doing routine but necessary work to provide treatment for those in need of it. While he might resist any analogizing, it is sincerely easy to say that Calhoun's body of work, which is only fortified by revelations of divine love, also offers care and company.”
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以英国隐修者朱利安·诺里奇的早期英文女性著作为统一主题，从日常生活的微小启示中提取灵感。十四首短小精悍的曲目呈现出柔和而富有气泡感的电子声响，音色质地如同太妃糖般具有触感，旋律试探前行而不张扬。音乐在催眠式长篇与即时捕捉的瞬息之间寻找平衡，聚焦于转瞬即逝的情感时刻。创作者白天在肿瘤治疗中心工作，将平凡与意义的交织作为美学核心，专辑流露出怀疑与寻找并存的开放态度，既私密又具普世关怀。作品不依赖炫技，而是以克制的细节编织出持久的亲密感。

items.body:
Reissue of the debut by A.G. Cook & Danny L Harle’s earliest duo, Dux Content, initially dispensed on Gamsonite, a predecessor of P.C. Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card.

Scrolling back to what now feels like a distant world - the up-for-grabs edges of early 2010s - ‘Lifestyle’ maps out formative aspects of the two producers, still relatively fresh from music studies at Goldsmiths, and making their mark in a burgeoning “internet music” scene. Of course they’re both now chart-topping songwriters/producers with credits for Charli xcx, Dua Lipa, Oklou, et al, but here they’re positively bubbling over with wild, yet disciplined, fusions of upfront hard dance with jazz, contemporary classical and pop that, with the benefit of hindsight, place them in a contemporaneous cultural slipstream with likes of Cracksmurf/T C F or James Ferraro, and soon-to-be spar, SOPHIE.

‘Lifestyle’ is the sound of two minds scything thru cultures and sounds they grew up with - Harle coming from a family background spanning his Geordie dad, John Harle’s BBC scores and early taste for makina’s stacked melodies - and bonding over a shared love of Captain Beefheart, Archie Sheep, and Tim & Eric, all evident in their grasp of shiny, commercial hooks and complex rhythm wrapped up with daft grin and wink. Shake a wand anywhere and you’ll hit a mad one, from the crazed midi piano house of ‘Voice of an Angel’, thru the jazz-fink of ‘City Break’ and ‘Hero Next Door’, free wheeling jazz trance of ‘Heart of Death’ and pitch bent panpipes of ‘Business Class’.
items._genre: experimental electronic / hyperpop / internet music / electro-house / hard dance
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是PC Music创始人A.G. Cook与Danny L Harle早期二人组Dux Content的处女作再版，由Gamsonite发行，可视为日后厂牌的雏形。两位制作人从Goldsmiths音乐研究毕业后，在2010年代初的互联网音乐场景中起步，将makina、硬核舞曲、爵士与当代古典等多种脉络并置重组，塑造出兼具野性与纪律性的声音设计。专辑呈现出将闪亮商业hook与复杂节奏包裹在一起的特质，融合如迷幻中频钢琴house、自由爵士trance、变调排箫等奇趣元素。乐评将其置于与Cracksmurf、James Ferraro、SOPHIE同期同源的文化语境中，追溯两人从地下实验走向Charli xcx、Dua Lipa等顶级制作人的成长轨迹。对关注实验电子与跨类型融合的听众而言，是一份了解hyperpop美学源头的重要文献。

items.body:
The Mitteleuropa enigma is strong on the 2nd original LP by Pablo’s Eye for Stroom, commanding attention to noctilucent, cinematic synth scapes laced with hand-played drums and poetry that plays out like a waking dream.

Active since ’89, the rotating assembly of Pablo’s Eye, headed by Axel Libeert, have plotted a unique course thru the backwaters of art rock, ambient, fantasy soundtrack music, and whatever else they fancy, leading to a pair of retrospectives on Stroom in 2018-19, plus the cult EP ‘Bardo For Pablo’, and fresh material on ‘The Light Was Sharp, Our Eyes Were Closed’ (2024).

Here represented by Marie Mandi, Luc Laret, Thierry Royo, Richard Skinner, Axel Libeert, and Ludwig Lapauw on ‘Everything You Give Away’, they follow noses for a typically low slung and resoundingly atmospheric album primed to seduce anyone in its path, as they stealthily proceed from the nightfall of ‘Walking the Line’, reminding us of DAAC, to the blushed choral pads and trip hop bass of ‘Reverie’ and Reese bass-gilded centrepiece ‘A dash of raspberry’, and ultimately the widescreen departure of ‘October ’75’. 

Trés classy.

items._cn_summary: Pablo's Eye 带来第二张正式专辑，由 Axel Libeert 领衔的轮换阵容自1989年活跃至今，融合艺术摇滚、环境音乐与幻想式电影配乐。整张专辑氛围低沉浓郁，从夜幕降临般的开篇曲过渡到合唱垫音与trip hop低音交织的段落，再到Reese低音点缀的中段佳作，最终以宽银幕式的离场曲收束。手奏鼓点与合成器音景相互渗透，诗歌般的歌词如同清醒之梦般展开。比利时厂牌Stroom发行的这张作品延续了乐队的跨风格实验路线，将中欧神秘气质注入每首曲目。评论以简洁的'极有品味'作结，突显其在氛围营造与跨类型融合上的成熟度。

items._cn_summary: 这是一张1971年由Ragnar Johnson与Ralph Harrisson在埃塞俄比亚实地录制的音乐合辑，收录了独具特色的弹拨竖琴begena演奏、阿姆哈拉语诗歌吟唱以及迷人的长笛舞曲等多元传统音乐形式。录音捕捉了那个时代埃塞俄比亚民间音乐的原生态风貌，兼具学术田野录音的档案价值与音乐本身的艺术感染力。与Death Is Not The End厂牌此前发行的begena系列合辑相比，本辑视野更为开阔，在保持亲密质感的同时展现了更丰富的音乐光谱。这些录音既是民族音乐学的珍贵文献，也让现代听众得以感受埃塞俄比亚传统音乐的独特韵味与精神性，适合对世界音乐与田野录音感兴趣、具有开放聆听习惯的听众深入品鉴。

items._cn_summary: 娜塔莉娅·贝利斯是一位环境音乐作曲家，她带领一支来自爱尔兰的弦乐与打击乐五重奏组合，以爱尔兰莱特里姆的一片田野为灵感，构建出一幅关于鸟类与树木自然逻辑的声音景观。整张专辑是一件慢速燃烧的长篇作品，以她聆听黑鸫黎明合唱为起点，与当地农民关于鸟类播种树木的对话为延伸，将大提琴、小提琴、小提琴与打击乐的简约编制融入环境氛围与当代古典的写作逻辑中。作品带有明显的爱尔兰地方色彩，将自然观察转化为作曲素材，以五重奏的克制编排呈现沉思式的声响质地，既不是传统民谣的叙事套路，也超越了常规当代古典的结构框架，而是试图用乐器模拟田野间生物的声学关系，属于跨界的实验性环境作品。

items.body: Venetian maestro Gigi Masin, active since the early tape era, threads MIDI phrasing with soft techno patterns and submerged tonal layers. A sense of persistence rather than grief alone Gigi Masin returns with Movement, his first solo LP since Calypso, shifting ambient into pulse-driven structures and sequenced motion. Out on May 29th via Sacred Bones, Movement reframes ambient as physical music, built for shared space, where loops, low frequencies, and sustained tones guide the body as much as the ear. “Deception Dance” has been the first excerpt. This new album is significantly influenced by the recent collaboration with sound designer Rod Modell and also benefits from Anacleto Vitolo’s excellent mastering work. “UMI” and its minimalist style add a touch of coolness that doesn’t feel cold, transporting you to a chill corner of a sweaty room, the same space shared with the seven-and-a-half-minute “Deception Dance,” a minimal techno track that, with snippets of alien-sounding phrases. “Lost,” is dedicated to the disappearance of his wife: an act of love and tenderness conveyed through a synthesized trumpet, representing a “love letter that was no longer received and was thrown into the river.” The more rhythmic tracks (such as “Golden” or ) have been interpreted as a tribute/exploration that blends and reinterprets techno-funk sounds, Balearic bossa nova (in the vein of Manuel Göttsching), and classic Balearic influences. In 2007, the beloved Italian composer lost his entire musical archive in a house flood, forcing him to put music on the back burner for a while. These events could have disrupted his work entirely. Instead, Masin continued to create. The album reflects a sense of persistence rather than grief alone. There is emotion present, but it is expressed through subtle shifts rather than dramatic gestures. Movement is available on Sacred Bones. [Bandcamp] Movement by Gigi Masin  The post Gigi Masin :: Movement (Sacred Bones) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: 意大利威尼斯作曲家Gigi Masin暌违多年推出新专辑，将环境音乐从静态氛围转向有律动的序列结构。专辑融合MIDI编曲、柔质techno节拍与低频延音层，强调身体性与空间感，适合共享聆听而非独处沉思。与声音设计师Rod Modell的合作及Anacleto Vitolo的母带处理为作品增添了层次。曲目涵盖极简techno、合成小号抒情段落以及对Balearic与techno-funk的重新诠释。2007年因洪水失去全部音乐档案的经历并未终止创作，反而塑造了一种以持续性而非悲恸为核心的美学——情绪通过微妙位移而非戏剧化姿态表达。Sacred Bones厂牌发行，整体定位介于实验电子与俱乐部文化之间，具有独立厂牌的地下气质。
