items.body: Across the vast American sprawl, post-punk and darkwave have taken root in cities throughout the country, with each local scene giving the music its own character. Among the rising bands within that wider movement, Casket Cassette and Stare Away represent two distant geographic poles: Los Angeles and New York City, the City of Angels and Gotham, relentless sunshine and after-dark intensity. This summer, the bands have closed nearly 3,000 miles of continental distance on Casket Cassette’s Reducer Tour, the Los Angeles project’s first headlining run. Constant Laval Williams and Ben Nelson first became friends when Stare Away joined a Casket Cassette bill at Sip Studios in Jersey City, where they discovered common ground in Joy Division’s rhythmic force and Ian Curtis’s songwriting, as well as recovery, poetry, and the desire to exorcise personal damage through catharsis of a crowd. Both artists entered the tour with their most substantial releases to date. Casket Cassette’s third album, Reducer, released June 12, turns experiences of erasure, constriction, recovery, and the aftermath of the Los Angeles fires into a ten-song study of what survives when a life and community have been pared back. Post-Punk.com followed the record’s development through Kiss Me Awake and Show Me a Sign, songs that brought Williams’s doomed romanticism into sharper electronic relief. On July 31, Stare Away released its seven-song debut, In Absence, via à La Carte Records, drawing on Nelson’s seclusion after sobriety, the depths of addiction, and relationships that continued to exert their pull. Its closing track, Familiar, gave those concerns one of the album’s most immediate expressions. Onstage, their geographical and musical differences sharpen the pairing. Casket Cassette channels the strange darkness that flourishes beneath Los Angeles sunshine through electronic pressure and doomed pop melody, while Stare Away draws on Gotham’s nocturnal velocity with tensile bass, urgent guitar, and the close physical charge of an early post-punk club. As the tour enters its final stretch, Post-Punk.com spoke with Williams and Nelson about the records that guided Reducer and In Absence, the friendship behind the tour, the cultures of their respective cities, and the collaboration already waiting beyond the final date: Ben, in absence, feels like a reference to the terms “In Memoriam” or “To Absent Friends”. What kind of absence does the title refer to, and what emotional or thematic thread holds the album together? The record is a massive reflection on the past couple years of my life. I definitely secluded myself from a lot of aspects of living in New York City so I could just focus and make progress on better finding myself after getting sober. I just disappeared for a while from going out and was working full-time at a job I absolutely hated. I looked at myself & how insane the state of the world currently is, and put everything into my craft to reflect my own mysteries, questions & realizations of isolation, depths of addiction, and relationships I’ve had that were very important to me. I think when you put your heart into something physical and artistic, people will truly relate rather than follow like a cheap social media posting scheme and will feel much more fruitful and fulfilling in the end. I feel like I discovered more about myself throughout the process of writing this record than I ever would if I hadn’t. The title track sums up the entire record and each following track dissects it in its own way musically and lyrically. Sitting with Mike Morello in the studio and putting so much time and emotion into each song really tied it all up with a bow. Ben, which artists, records, or musical periods were foremost in your mind while making In Absence? Or writers and filmmakers perhaps? To really narrow it down, New Order’s “Movement” demos and writing sessions, The Cure’s “Faith” home demos, and The Sound’s “Jeopardy” record are in my everyday rotation. When it came down to pure influence, I really wanted to write from a direction as a band involved in the first wave with a maturing mid-80s attitude. The sculpting behind what defined an emerging underground genre is what I’ll always strive for when writing. Experimental films and beatnik writers of the late 50s and 60s called me to think more of vulnerability in expression when it came down to writing the lyrics. Ben, was there one song that unlocked the direction of In Absence and helped you understand what the rest of the record needed to become? “I Can’t Escape Myself” by the Sound. Truly a masterpiece of a track in my opinion. The daily hysteria of living life on life’s terms regardless of situation or control over one’s ability to have an answer for everything that shapes our identities and emotions is kind of a beauty in a sense, which makes us all unique in our own ways. The album art shot by Julie Lodhy really captured that reflection literally. Constant, what first set Reducer in motion, and how did the album develop from that initial idea into the finished record? I’d been spending most of my time focusing on crafting standout singles (Bouquet, Broken Tomorrow, etc.), and I wanted to return to another cohesive project. Specifically, for album #3, I wanted to respond to the erasure, reduction, and alienation I’d been feeling after returning home to LA from graduate school at the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, and in the wake of the LA fires. In a short period of time, my community of friends and my childhood home had both burned, shrunk, or vanished. It was a period of interpersonal, mental, and physical loss. I first explored these themes in the context of inward reflection, and then expanded into an examination of my past and my relationship to others. I also chose to incorporate increasingly poetic elements (such as references to Robert Lowell’s Skunk Hour in Kiss Me Awake, a poem in the interlude, and various lyrics that leaned more deeply into nuanced metaphor). The instruments ended up expressing rage, loss, and existential claustrophobia via the use of heavy basslines and aggressive drums, coupled with ethereal anthemic synths and the occasional heartfelt guitar line. What made me fall in love with the darkwave and post-punk genres to begin with was their ability to honestly express pain and darkness while also transfiguring that same pain into something beautiful and danceable. I can only hope this new album achieved that same duality. Constant, the word “reducer” suggests compression, subtraction, or stripping something to its essential form. What does the title mean to you, and how does it relate to the album’s songs? I think that you summed it up nicely. Like the choke-chain collar in the cover art, the title reflects a feeling of constriction (a minimization of self, community and environment). If you have the kind of brain that I have, life can sometimes feel like a series of “reductions” almost like pruning a bonsai tree to try to stay “right sized.” This has always been the case for me (especially as someone in recovery), but to have those reductions unwillingly extend into the world around me was intense. I think the songs all mirror this differently. I tried to let them be eclectic; sometimes disparate elements in conversation with one another are more comprehensive than similar elements. On songs like Kiss Me Awake and Melting Angels, there’s a wide-open purgatorial feeling that’s at odds with poignant, pared-down lyrics. A song like Pacific Coast Highway (PTSD) is a bittersweet memory, a bleeding echo of a whole. Show Me a Sign and Becoming burst past constriction into raw expressions of existential energy (etc.). Harmoniously, the album was mixed by Matia Simovich at Infinite Power Studios, who works almost exclusively with analog equipment. The process of mixing with analog machines is also a reduction of the nebulous revisions and additions of modern DAWs; when effects were baked into the stems, they were made singular and permanent. The same is true for Matia’s raw, minimalistic approach to tracking vocals on songs I recorded in-studio such as Becoming. The stems of some songs like Elegy were compressed together onto tape, and then re-digitized. Constant, which artists and records exerted the strongest influence on Reducer, and where can you hear those influences entering the album? There is always a plethora of artists within (and outside of) the genre influencing me. These, of course, include the giants whose footsteps we walk in (ie. Joy Division, The Cure, Bauhaus, Siouxsie, etc.) as well as the peers I have walking beside me (check out my Spotify playlist for reference). If I had to narrow it down for this specific album, I’d say: Charlotte Sometimes by The Cure, But Not Tonight by Depeche Mode (specifically the intro), the body of work by Sad Madona (who I’ve done two collaborations with (including on Reducer), and who I’ve been hanging out with when I visit the EU), the music of my buddy Jamison (aka Gossip Cult), indie and indie-adjacent bands I used to listen to when I was a kid (like Beach Fossils, Surf Curse, The Drums, etc,), The Smiths, Atmosphere by Joy Division, Crystal Castles, experimental acid/trance/house music I used to dance to at illegal warehouse raves downtown, Nitzer Ebb, Pagliacci by Leoncavallo, and various movie soundtracks. As a result, songs like Pacific Coast Highway (PTSD) blend post-punk and indie/alternative, while songs like Show Me a Sign or Apathy are darkwave with elements of electronica and EBM. All of these influences have allowed me to move in a new direction while staying true to my voice. Constant, you are also a poet, photographer, and filmmaker. How did those other disciplines shape the lyrics, imagery, or structure of Reducer? For me, all these disciplines come from the same source but are expressed in different ways, each appropriate for different moments/needs. They all allow us as human beings to try to source meaning from existence and our universe; a meaning we will never fully reach, but a beautiful process regardless. Photography and film rely on choice of subject and composition to craft visual narrative or provoke thought, while music relies on a similar, auditory gut-instinct. These instincts are also involved in poetry, but the act of writing and editing a poem requires a more microscopic cartography; everything must belong, every word must connect, every image must work against or for the conceit of the poem. Poetry is my first love. I’m obsessed with it. There’s a beautiful anarchy to it, yet an intentionality that I don’t find to be fully true in music or photography. Sometimes my lyrics are hyper poetic, and sometimes I want a break from the intense scrutiny required of poetry. Sometimes I just want to write an immediately understandable or quasi-cliché lyric for the catharsis of that immediacy; just want to say “I love you” or “I miss you” and not “your shadow lingers in the wake of my delinquent dreams.” Coming out of the Writers’ Workshop and being in the process of finishing my debut collection of poetry, poetry played a much larger role in this album than in the past. As I previously mentioned, there is a full poem in the Interlude; songs like Elegy and Kiss Me Awake both use rhyme schemes (or non-rhyming free-verse) in their lyrics and poetic imagery that is a new frontier for the fusion of poetry and music for me. I have a very vivid imagination; it can be very cinematic at times. I daydream a lot. When I was writing Reducer, photography and cinematography also informed the songs for sure—if I can’t imagine a visual narrative in my head while listening back to a song, then it’s probably not a good song. Structurally, I always want my albums to have a narrative arc as well. In the case of Reducer, I wanted to start with a feeling of stasis and constriction that then erupted into defiant forward movement. Constant and Ben, how did the two of you first meet, and what were your initial impressions of one another, both personally and as musicians? Ben: We met at the Jersey City date of his first US tour with Blood Club and dustbowlchampion at Sip Studios, it was so cool to be able to meet from being on complete opposite sides of the country, everyone was so inviting and kind and it was awesome being able to appreciate each others music. It was like going to a new school and kicking it off with another kid in class with similar interests. Constant: Ben and I met a few years ago on my first-ever national tour with Blood Club and Dustbowlchampion. I had already been aware of Ben’s music after finding it online and would religiously listen to “My Cathedral” and “Something Strange” in my car on the way to work, so I was psyched when Ben was booked to play with all of us in Jersey City. I think we hit it off immediately; I could tell Ben just got it, it being the reason we all do what we do as artists. It’s really cool when you meet someone and are on the same wavelength. Stare Away. Photo by Constant Williams Constant and Ben, did you initially connect through any shared bands, records, or influences, and what helped that first connection develop? Ben: Definitely comparing our distinguished sounds to similar bands we both enjoy, I think Joy Division would be a top example because we both love Ian Curtis’ writing from a poetic standpoint, we did hit the exhibit in New York City together which was an awesome experience. I always learn of new books and readings to pick up from him. I also think it’s because I am a bassist and he came from a background of being a drummer, so I think a lot of bands that have that heavy foundation of rhythm sections drove a lot of our similar musical interests. Constant: For sure, I think most people who make music similar to us can connect over a shared love of many of the same bands (like the ones I mentioned before). I think it also helped that we both come to music at a poetic and existential angle, and we both could relate in terms of recovery from substances and the perspective shift that is required. Constant and Ben, what first made you want to collaborate musically, and when did the idea of touring together enter the conversation? We haven’t collaborated yet but we definitely have a song in the works. I think every time we’ve seen each other, we’ve thrown around the idea of touring together because we love each other’s music, and it especially made sense now that both of us are with BLCKJEANS. Ben, what appeals to you most about Reducer, and which song from the record do you find yourself returning to most often? I think Constants approach on the arrangements were genius. The drum breaks feel lyrical, the combination of synth selections and vocal melodies reached a part of this genre that hasn’t been touched upon yet, and classic Casket Cassette elements cultivated into his best work. My favorite part of all this is watching and listening as an artist grows musically. It’s hard to put my finger on a single song because each song has its own unique skeleton, but I have to go with “Apathy” as the track that’s always running through my head on this record. Constant, what do you enjoy most about In Absence, and which song on the album has become your personal favorite? Beyond how catchy and danceable its songs are, I love how authentic and genuine the album is. I also really enjoy the combination of quintessential 80’s New Wave sounds with dark Post-Punk melodies. The title track and Faithless Hum are my top favorites. Constant and Ben, your music shares certain post-punk and darkwave foundations while retaining two distinct identities. What do you think makes the bands complement each other so well on the same bill? Ben: I think our high-energy performances are what make this tour so special; the riffs throughout the night keep the atmosphere intense with movement and bring a great amount of nostalgia you feel at a goth club or punk show that you can’t capture at other shows. Our deep connection with the fans is what’s most important to me, hearing how the music can move through the audience and watching kids get lost in their dancing with their eyes closed while we’re playing on stage is so cool being able to resonate that from the stage. Constant: I think we complement each other because we both bring a similar energetic performance style, matching high energy with a candid sincerity. Ben’s music leans more towards post-punk with moments of darkwave, while my music leans more towards darkwave with moments of post-punk. I think that also creates a “yin and yang” effect for our live shows; two sides of the same coin. Casket Cassette. Photo by Aaron Jay Young Constant, you come from Los Angeles, while Ben is based in New York City. How have the music scenes and cultures of those cities shaped your respective projects, and what similarities do you recognize between them? And what do you think is different? Ben: I think New York City’s music scene is so diverse, which makes it such a beautiful and thriving location for musicians and showgoers. You can hit a punk show, an electronic show, hardcore show, or jazz club in the same borough in the same night. It’s wicked, I love it. I think LA is quite the same besides the traffic haha, but I think the diversity of people and genres is the best and most important similarity of both cities, keeping live music thriving. New York City in general has a million places to find and take inspiration from. Taking late night subway rides can create a huge narrative story in its own way, walking in the parks and seeing all different types of fashion and taking everyone’s unique sense of expression and sensing love and unfortunate disparities throughout the air can present all kinds of thoughts and ideas to put down on paper, it becomes its own dimension and reality that spews inspiration for lyrics and especially beat and rhythm. The nightlife through dive bars and street festivities is an overwhelming resource of artistic relation. You can simply sit in a moment, look around, and take in so much that you can’t find anywhere else. I try to take the mood and energy of wherever I was that night or night before to the writing process to resemble the city’s grit and hardstyle energy that keeps it alive. Constant: I think growing up in Los Angeles has informed my music a lot. There’s a strange duality to the shiny movie stars, warm beaches, and perpetual sunshine that is surrounded by industrial decay, violence, and broken dreams. I think my music has a similar duality, being both deeply sad and deeply danceable. That’s a strange combo that (I hope) works. It definitely reflects how I grew up and who I am; I never truly fit into any one box. On the contrary, despite being visually more gothic and less “shiny” than LA, I feel as though the scene might be a bit less substantial in size in New York City, but I only know a little from my limited experience. It has always made me laugh that the places with the most goths are often the ones that punish us with bright sunlight (ie. Los Angeles, Mexico City, San Antonio, etc., with the exception of Chicago). I love New York, and I do think there is a kinship between the two cities, and certainly they are two of the most important musical hubs in the world. Constant and Ben, what are you each most excited about on this run, and what kind of experience do you hope audiences take away from seeing both projects in the same room? Ben: I’m really stoked to finally play these new songs live and also give the fans a chance to sing the songs that got us here with us. My absolute favorite part is inspiring younger showgoers to keep pushing their craft; the young musicians are the main reason I do this 100%. I started going to shows around 12-13 years old at VFWs and want to relive how I felt when people rushed to the stage to snag the mic from the vocalist to scream the lyrics. We want to go against the grain as much as possible so we get sweaty with everyone on stage with us during ‘Parting Ways’. It just started out of a last-minute call-up on our first show in San Diego so I just wanted to try and accomplish that every single night regardless of the size of the audience. I was pretty nervous at first, but I know the fans have such a fun time being able to dance underneath the lights with us, and that’s what matters the most. I hope the audience can take away a fresh new ear for Post-Punk music and can feel like they’re at a Factory or CBGB show. I just want people to feel free in a safe space and take home an amazing show experience. Constant: I’m excited to play shows with Stare Away and all our awesome local openers because I know the audience is going to have a great experience! As my first headliner tour, I’m also really excited to get to play a longer set for fans; I’m always bummed when someone comes up to say hi and is sad that I didn’t play a specific song; hopefully having a fuller set mitigates some of that disappointment. Another favorite part of tour for me is meeting the amazing people who listen to my music; none of this would be possible without them, and they mean everything to me. All I want is for them to have a night where they can let go and enjoy themselves during these crazy times. Constant and Ben, once the tour is over and both albums have had time to settle into the world, what does each of you have planned for 2027, and do you envision further collaborations? Ben: As soon as we get back, I plan on just getting right back to constructing the direction of the next record. I want to find the perfect hybrid kit to add to our live shows and just make something different. I feel like a lot of bands just get trapped in the same sound, playing the same riffs. I definitely want to get my head into a new book and maybe pick up some weird new hobby, but I think I just want to challenge myself towards a new direction to take Stare Away. Constant: I recently won a literary award, and as a result I will be releasing a book of poetry in 2027 called Elegy with Beautiful Child, available for preorder from Milkweed Editions. My lifelong dream (even before music) has always been to publish a book of poetry, so this is a really important moment in my life! There is also a Stare Away x Casket Cassette song in the works, and Ben and I are good friends, so it’s definitely not the last you’ll be hearing from both of us.§ Casket Cassette’s Reducer is out now. Listen below, and Order Here. REDUCER by Casket Cassette Stare Away’s In Absence is out now. Listen below and Order Here. In Absence by Stare Away The end of the Reducer tour leaves both artists with fresh work already taking shape. Nelson plans to begin developing the next Stare Away record as soon as he returns to New York, introducing a hybrid drum kit while pushing the project toward unfamiliar methods. Williams will turn toward the January 2027 publication of Elegy with Beautiful Child, his debut poetry collection and winner of the 2025–26 Jake Adam York Prize. A Stare Away and Casket Cassette song is also underway, extending a friendship that began on a shared bill into the studio. Before those plans take over, Casket Cassette and Stare Away have eight dates remaining together on Casket Cassette’s Reducer Tour. The itinerary continues August 12 at Beat Kitchen in Chicago, followed by Minneapolis, Denver, Salt Lake City, Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco before their shared run closes August 22 at Summer Fox Brewing – Tower in Fresno. Casket Cassette and Stare Away Reducer Tour Dates: August 12 — Chicago, IL — Beat Kitchen August 13 — Minneapolis, MN — 7th St Entry August 15 — Denver, CO — Skylark Lounge August 16 — Salt Lake City, UT — Kilby Court August 18 — Seattle, WA — The Black Lodge August 19 — Portland, OR — Holocene August 21 — San Francisco, CA — Kilowatt August 22 — Fresno, CA — Summer Fox Brewing – Tower Follow Casket Cassette: Instagram Spotify YouTube TikTok Bandcamp Follow Stare Away: Instagram Spotify YouTube TikTok Bandcamp The post Between Fallen Angels and Gotham Nights — An Interview With Casket Cassette and Stare Away on the “Reducer” Tour appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: 本文是一次围绕Casket Cassette与Stare Away两支乐队联合巡演的访谈式报道。前者来自洛杉矶，发行第三张专辑《Reducer》，以电子压力与宿命式流行旋律为底色，将火灾创伤、自我缩减与社群重建转化为十首作品的减法美学；后者来自纽约，七月三十一号由à La Carte Records发行首张专辑《In Absence》，以紧致贝斯、急迫吉他与早期后朋俱乐部能量回应当事人戒断后的隐居、沉溺与未了关系。两位主创因Joy Division的节奏力量与Ian Curtis的词作而结缘，巡演地理与音乐的差异形成互补：洛杉矶阳光下的异常黑暗，与纽约的夜间速度彼此对照。文章以巡演即将结束为时间节点，穿插二人共同影响的唱片、巡演背后的友谊、两城文化差异，以及后续合作计划。文本偏向访谈与背景介绍，对音乐本身的声响分析较为有限。

items.body: Karlsruhe, Germany industrial death-wave trio Bleak Monday has released a video for Shelter, a single issued on Bandcamp on July 31, 2026. The track is drawn from Bleak Monday’s upcoming debut album, “Bad Music”, which does not yet have a confirmed release date. The video for “Shelter” was directed by Natascha Gaballo. It is the latest visual release from the band, which has built its catalogue independently since forming in December 2022. “Shelter” follows Bleak Monday’s 2024 single “Human Needs”, released December 13, 2024, and the band’s earlier EP “flies”. The new track continues the project’s industrial death-wave sound, pairing distorted guitar and synth textures with vocalist Kim Ryder’s delivery. About Bleak Monday Bleak Monday formed in Karlsruhe, Germany, in December 2022. The trio is made up of Kim Ryder (vocals), Yann Lauer (guitar and feedback) and Sebastian “Hubu” Huber (synths, drums and bass). The band began playing live in early 2023 and has since shared stages with acts including Das Kinn, Nils Keppel, The Body and Ministry. Bleak Monday released its debut EP, “flies”, followed by the single “Human Needs” on December 13, 2024. Both releases, along with “Shelter”, are self-released through the band’s Bandcamp page. “Shelter” is presented as an early single from Bleak Monday’s forthcoming debut album, “Bad Music”.

items.body:
The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

items.body: Review by Agnenrecords — (This review originally appeared on my website progblog.co.uk on 21st December 2021)Locanda delle Fate's Forse Le Lucciole Non Si Amano Pi� (Polydor, 1977) is quite rightly regarded as one of the best progressivo italiano albums of the 70s but it is also a classic example of the right record at the wrong time, as it was released when symphonic prog and long suites in general had begun to be ignored by a new generation of music fans. They disbanded in 1980.The resurgent interest in progressive rock in the 1990s, reappraising the music of a generation before, was sufficiently broad to include Locanda delle Fate, and their debut album was released on CD, with bonus tracks in 1990. The group reformed in 1996 and released the more straightforward rock CD Homo Homini Lupus three years later, then regrouped in 2010 and played their farewell tour in 2017.One of the main songwriters was Michele Conta (fifth from the left in the Forse Le Lucciole Non Si Amano Pi� inner gatefold group photo) who joined the band as a pianist just aged 17. Conta was largely responsible for the romantic influences, hinting at the keyboard work of Tony Banks but perhaps more accurately, creating a sound that fitted the vocals of Leonardo Sasso and generating comparisons with the music of Banco del Mutuo Soccorso. Conta was born in the Piemonte city of Asti, where at the age of 10 he began studying piano at the Giuseppe Verdi Music Institute under the guidance of organist and composer Giuseppe Peirolo, later moving to the Antonio Vivaldi Conservatory in Alessandria, a city 37km due east of Asti, to continue his studies with the concert pianist Maria Gachet.He gave up a career in music and instead trained to become a doctor, and continues to practise medicine in his home city to this day. In 2012, AltRock released a Locanda delle Fate CD of tracks written at the same time as but not included on Forse Le Lucciole Non Si Amano Pi�, recorded by the 2010 incarnation of the band and supplemented with excerpts from a gig at Asti's Teatro Alfieri on November 21st 1977, a performance which does include Conta.In one of the most unbelievable examples of sampling (even stranger than 50 Cent using Me and You for Other Days from I Pooh's 1973 album Parsifal for his song Everytime I Come Around), rapper/producer Dr. Dre used Conta's piano arpeggio from Vendesi Saggezza throughout For The Love of Money on the 2015 CD Compton, which was nominated for Best Rap Album at the 2015 Grammy Awards; the film Straight Outta Compton inspired by the CD was also nominated for the best screenplay at the Oscars. It should be said that Conta has been recognised as the copyright holder.Conta's love of music remained and he continued to compose, eventually deciding to record some of the compositions with the help of the sound engineer and co-arranger Simone Lampedone. The CD Endless Nights was released on AMS records in 2019, a collection of original compositions built up since he left the band. He admits it took a long time to complete this album but he has been working as a doctor throughout. Conta has stated that Endless Nights reflects the changes of the last 40-50 years, from the golden age of prog when form and structure in music were important, to the present day with its immediacy and modern music production values. When you first hear the instrumental � nell'aria (It's in the Air) you're transported back to 1977, with the piano melody and the staccato guitar phrasing providing a sonic link to A Volte un Istante di Quiete. The track also provides an insight into the quality of his collaborators, with Gavin Harrison (Porcupine Tree, King Crimson) on drums.With You on the Walk of my Life has a similar feel and is of a very similar length to � nell'aria though this track features vocals, delivered by guitarist Ermanno Brignolo and sung in English. There's more synthesizer, but still lots of gorgeous piano.Notte Infinita (title track Endless Nights) is another instrumental, but this provides a degree of contrast because it has a more modern sounding palette, with synthesizer given more of a lead role. The song builds up following a choral keyboard section, slows briefly before resuming the up-tempo, uplifting feel with guitar and synthesizer sharing the melody.Growin' Up is another track with a distinctive Costa-penned melody line reminiscent of Locanda delle Fate and lots more piano. The arrangement varies between modern sounding during the vocal passages, sung in English, and a structure reflecting his writing in the 70s. In Riva Al Mondo (On the Shores of the World) is sung in Italian. Beginning with tolling bells, it's played at a slower tempo with acoustic guitar, lending a prog-romantic feeling. The keyboard work is primarily piano lead and the whole piece is much more orchestrated. The pace is picked up around the middle of the track, and there's some restrained electric guitar before the tempo moves down a gear for another vocal section, then picks up again before slowing and fading.Fiori Nascoti (Hidden Flowers) begins with piano and cello, a reflective orchestral introduction followed by a modern sounding break, before the melody is introduced and rather like the preceding track, the pace increases and slows as layers of instruments are added and subtracted. The vocals are short and at the very end of the piece, which ends with a piano flourish.Overall, the album is uplifting, positive-sounding and has a brightness that's difficult to define. The beautiful piano playing provides a link back to Locanda delle Fate and I'd recommend this album to any fan of Forse Le Lucciole Non Si Amano Pi�, but Endless Nights manages to occupy territory shared with modern progressivo italiano acts. It doesn't sound like a solo album either, because the songs have been sympathetically arranged for the different musicians and their respective instruments. It may have taken a long time to make, but it was most definitely worth it.An easy 4 stars

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自意大利前卫摇滚（Rock Progressivo Italiano）传统，作者Michele Conta曾是Locanda delle Fate乐队的钢琴手与主要作曲者，乐队以七十年代浪漫化的交响前卫风格著称，Conta的键盘写作受Tony Banks及Banco del Mutuo Soccorso影响。《Endless Nights》是Conta搁置音乐多年、从医之余持续创作的成果，2019年由AMS Records发行，作品延续了意大利老派交响前卫的浪漫抒情路线，以钢琴为主导，结合人声与管弦化编配。乐评花大量篇幅回顾Conta的生平、教育背景、Locanda delle Fate的历史，以及他早年钢琴琶音被Dr. Dre采样用于《Compton》的版权事件。整体而言，这是一张怀旧色彩浓厚、风格保守的意大利老派前卫续作，缺乏明显的实验性或跨界突破，主要面向老派前卫乐迷，对追求前卫实验与跨界融合的听众而言吸引力有限。

items.body: Review by alainPP — Anneke Van Giersbergen launches her second LP with a powerful sense of grief, a song about life before love."Fade In Fade Out" features flawless piano and vocals, a contained explosion of folk-rock-pop reminiscent of The Gathering with its rich synths. The latent break, a fierce, chaotic, progressive riff, is punctuated by a captivating saxophone in a dreamlike crescendo. An acoustic reprise showcases her inimitable voice as a ballad over a Southern-tinged guitar. "Handle Me With Care" boasts an electro beat, reminiscent of The Corrs, The Cranberries, and Blondie, with its distinctive drums; a minimalist new-wave pop sound. The saxophone returns, accompanied by a synth on Ultravox in a binary, danceable, and solemn mode."Red Sky" stands out for its perfect harmony between the phrased vocals and the minimalist instrumental, reminiscent of The White Stripes. The synth bass reminiscent of the Smashing Pumpkins evokes the 90s. Anneke drifts along without a care in the world, accompanied by a subtly lush orchestration, culminating in a bewitching, mantra-like folk vocal finale. "Sail Towards The Sun," a melancholic, poignant acoustic ballad brimming with emotion, recounts her farewell to her father and memories of sailing trips; drums and classical instruments accompany her angelic voice.Anneke van Giersbergen continues to showcase her angelic voice on this second installment of her triptych chronicling the loss of her parents.
items._cn_summary: Anneke van Giersbergen第二张个人专辑延续其三部曲主题，围绕失去父母的悲伤展开创作。专辑融合民谣、流行与少量前卫元素，钢琴与萨克管在多首歌中交替出现，为旋律增添层次感。编曲上借鉴了The Gathering的丰富合成器音色，并融入新浪潮节拍与原声吉他的民谣质感。歌词直面生死的告别主题，旋律抒情而克制，嗓音表现被视为专辑亮点。整体而言，这是一张以旋律与人声为核心的成熟作品，情感真挚但艺术突破有限，对于偏好前卫实验、爵士即兴或电子声响设计的听众而言，跨界幅度有限，偏向主流抒情流行受众。

items.body:
Proper, tracky, Chi-style budgers from the badboy Delroy Edwards, back to his vintage tricks on spiritual home L.A. Club Resource

The jakbeat is strong on this one, laid down direct and cruddy in the best sense with drum machines and  synths toiled into driving grooves that sound like they could have emerged during the mid ‘80s early years of house. Covering the spectrum of jakbeat flavours, he crosses from the title tune’s sultry swerve to hypnotic bass goop in ‘Put That’, cruising from the rude Adonis like keys of ‘Bring The House’ to a smart glimmer of FM synthesis smeared into ‘How’d You Do That’, and some Faces drums-style machine tickets on ‘Don’t Ya Know’, saving the punchiest tackle for the percolated funk and honk of ’Sweet Geese’, and dope nods to Gene Hunt on ‘House Blitz.’

items.body: Welp. Better late than never. It's Kvlt Kolvmn's a-bit-more-than-halfway through 2026 best of list! Strap into your frostiest pair of dungaroos. It's gonna get wild.Black metal has had a very curious year for me. While I would say about half of the records I've listened to in the genre have felt like all-time bangers, the other half have put me to sleep. So in honor of that, I'll be presenting half a top 10 list. You're welcome. More awesome, however, is Boeli's incredible top 10, which features a handful of records I had yet to hear prior to reading his selections. Let's just say that good taste abounds as his list unfolds.But no more delay. Here are our iciest picks of 2026 so far.Stay frosty.-Jonathan AdamsTop Albums of 2026 So FarJonathan’s ListSaidan - Fangdriller: Scars Beneath Memory’s WristAs made plain when I waxed ineloquent a few weeks ago regarding the benefits of embracing the cringe in your life, I’m a BIG fan of Saidan. I would contend that their four album run thus far is one of the most consistently impressive in recent black metal, with each record refining and tactfully building upon what came before. Given this dynamic, it should come as no surprise that Fangdriller: Scars Beneath Memory’s Wrist is not only the band’s most complete and fantastic album thus far, but also the best extreme music record of the year so far. For me, it’s not close. What Saidan manages to channel here is a superb blend of melodic black metal, punk aesthetics, and power metal speed (replete with memorable hooks, punchy breakdowns, and manically aggressive tremolo shred sessions). It’s a relatively unique mixture that works due to genuinely gorgeous songwriting, which allows each sound to coexist seamlessly and interdependently without giving the listener genre-bending whiplash. The base is always black metal, and Saidan writes like a black metal band expanding the margins of the genre’s template with tasteful aggression. But their inclusion of other styles only works to sharpen and deepen listeners’ immersion in the world they’re creating. There isn’t a dull moment on this thing, and I frequently find myself hitting play again immediately after “Memory” fades into static. It’s addictive as hell. And, ultimately, that’s what I want from a record. I want to be transported, invited into a sonic world that’s cohesive enough to keep my undivided attention, and varied enough to never feel stale. And that’s exactly what Saidan provide with this absolute gem of a record. It’s my favorite thing I’ve heard so far this year, and I have a hard time imagining it being supplanted. Melodic black metal perfection.  FANGDRILLER: Scars Beneath Memory's Wrist by Saidan Miserere Luminis - SideraSpeaking of immersion, few albums so far this year have gripped me to the degree that Sidera, the third full-length from Montreal-based Miserere Luminis, has. Man oh man is this an exquisite slab of melody-heavy and deeply atmospheric black metal. The compositions are simply fantastic, winding and building into a delicious labyrinth of emotionally devastating delight. The musicianship on display here is also superb, allowing these tracks to breathe in the appropriate places before laying the black metal hammer down to glorious effect. It’s a fantastic showing from a band that has yet to release a dud, and I cannot wait to see where they transport us next.  Sidera by Miserere Luminis Worm - NecropalaceOne of the most hyped and ballyhooed records of the first half of 2026, I was honestly ready to judge this thing pretty harshly given initial impressions I’d heard from friends around the band's shift in tone. Happy to say I was dead wrong, as Necropalace feels like the most natural direction in the world for Worm to go after spending significant time with it. In a similar vein to Fangdriller, this record is just FUN. The songwriting is gothic and propulsive, creating an almost theatrical atmosphere that’s deeply enjoyable to sit in. One would never have guessed at Worm’s doomy roots by hearing Necropalace, thus is its genuine quality as a black metal album. Can’t recommend it highly enough, and plan on giving this thing many more spins throughout the year.  Necropalace (24-bit HD audio) by Worm Ultha - A Light So DimUltha is one of the most unpredictable and strangely amazing collectives working in the black metal sphere today, and A Light So Dim is unequivocally their boldest experiment to date. Thankfully, it works on almost every level. While the tonal shifts may look jarring on paper, Ultha’s unique skill of pulling various sound tapestries and weaving them into a robust whole is on full display here, and there isn’t a thing I’d change about this record. It is a long journey, which may be off-putting to some. But rest assured the time will be well spent. This is my favorite of the group’s records so far and a musical odyssey well worth taking. Genuinely brilliant stuff from these German geniuses.  A Light So Dim by ULTHA Misotheist - De PinteWell, enough pansy ass beautiful/experimental poser black metal, amirite?? JK naturally. While I’m a huge fan of bands that push the black metal formula to the fringes of trve, I’m still a devotee of the core sonic nastiness that made this genre the pariah it is in the music world. Enter Misotheist and their brilliant fourth full-length outing De Pinte. Like your black metal with a hefty dose of buzzsaw dissonance and tremolo violence? You’re in luck! This record absolutely slays. The first three tracks in particular are nothing short of a masterclass in black metal done right, with enough audio violence to sate even the thirstiest fan. But it’s the records fourth cut that shows the band’s capabilities most notably, presenting a doomier side that slows down the tempo but never once minimizes the menace or aggression these enigmatic Norwegians are known for. It’s a brilliant album that has received many a spin from yours truly and a true highlight of 2026.  De Pinte by Misotheist Boeli’s Kvlt kolvmn Top 10: Where Kvltvre Goes to Feed the Vvltvres10. Einherjer - LifebloodBy virtue of another folk-tinged black metal indebted band not making the cut for reasons of probable sketch, Einherjer just made my top 10 spot even though it’s hardly been out long enough to form a proper opinion.One thing I can say without hesitation, is that I quite enjoy the Norwegian Viking metallers trajectory since I last actively listened to them about a decade ago. While Av Oss, For Oss was an occasionally engaging if fairly monotone exercise in mid-paced black metal, Lifeblood is a much more colorful and generally more dynamic and melodic affair, and while still rooted in black metal, the branches of its world tree sapling have grown to embrace heavy metal and folk metal more and more. I appreciate their more melodic and varied approach, and would appreciate it even more with some more tempo variation and a bit of judicious editing. That being said, there are times I long for this subgenre like no other, and this year Einherjer have been its prime deliverer so far.  Lifeblood by Einherjer 9. Burnt Lodge / Veytik - Anchors Plunged Off Helluland (Split)Another somewhat late entry, I had almost completely missed this release, and was well and truly excited when I saw Burnt Lodge had new stuff out. Their 2024 release Intergenerational Anamnesis is one of my favourite iterations of Native American Black Metal. This particular micro-genre is a particular favorite of mine, and alongside Blackbraid and Nechochwen, Burnt Lodge sits among its top practitioners. Had this been a full album,. And had I discovered it earlier, this one might have sat quite a bit higher.While I also quite enjoy Veytik’s thrasher, Hellenic and Obsequiaesque escapades, they have not yet managed to grab me like Burnt Lodge does.  Anchors Plunged Off Helluland (Split) by Burnt Lodge 8. Pure Wrath - Bleak Days AheadI shall lazily refer you to my previous musings on Pure Wrath’s latest in Mays Kvlt Kolvmn.  Bleak Days Ahead by Pure Wrath 7. Stormkeep - The Nocturnes of IswylmOn their latest, bombasically titled album, Stormkeep took me by storm out of the gate, although I’m not yet wholly sure they’ll remain in my top 10 for the year entire. I generally like my black metal adorned with a serious amount of low-end, contrary to its traditional sound. While Stormkeep toe the line of what I enjoy production wise, the mix of spooky whimsy, expansive songwriting and exhilarating choruses managed to perk my ears up considerably. The gruff, charming and incredibly catchy gang shouts of opener “The Taste of Immortal Blood” are choice as hell, and while I could do with some more hooks like those to get my very mortal blood a-pumping in the mid section before the last two tracks offer a convincing coda, I suspect the album may need some more time to gestate before it truly settles in. The Nocturnes Of Iswylm by Stormkeep 6. Antrisch - Expedition III: RenitenzpfadAtmospheric black metal might be one of the most oversaturated and justly maligned sub-genres, but when done right, it can also be one of it’s most powerful. Of course your definition of “right” will vary, and there are many roads to Rome. Enter Antrisch, whose take on the sub-genre is one I would use as a prime example of doing atmoblack well. Antrisch unleash a vicious, razor-sharp blackened assault, while adorning their music with a powerful, iterative concept of (historical) exploration of some very inhospitable environments.While previous album Die Passage’s arctic voyage was an obvious fit for Antrisch’s icy timbre, Renitenzpfad might be equally if not more exciting for its less obvious theme of the hardships endured and horrors dished out by Spanish colonisers in the Americas. With all of Antrisch’s biting venom, this time empowered by topical and tasteful atmospheric interludes, sampling and thematic instrumentation, they once again succeed in telling a story and immersing their audience in it, without ever diluting their vicious, energetic core sound. Smart, urgent, dynamic and varied, while remaining remarkably cohesive;  Expedition III is another successful iteration in these Germans’ discography. EXPEDITION III : Renitenzpfad by Antrisch 5. Ashbringer - SubglacialI stand by my original review; anything close to 2019s Absolution would have topped any list, whether Black Metal specific or not. Time has both made me lost sight of Subglacial (who releases an album in January, I ask you!?), while also softening my initial dashed expectations for another long-form atmoblack magnum opus. My expectations should not make for a good or bad album in the end, and Ashbringer’s wintry yet somehow warm and nostalgic 2026 release is absolutely a good album. Go listen to it if you haven’t yet, and then go listen to Absolution.  Subglacial by Ashbringer 4. Apolaustic - No Plenitude Without SufferingWere it not for a scheduling snafu on my end, I would have reviewed this melodic black metal gem in April, and could now get away with another short referral to something I wrote before. Alas, no luck. I did not, and you shall now suffer my relative plenitude. I picked up the promo for this album based on a promising single at the time, and was further pleasantly surprised by an album that proved deep and expansive enough that I was still forming a full opinion by teh time the review deadline slipped through my powerless fingers. A couple months later, I can tell you with full confidence that this is my favourite “pure” melodic black metal album of the year so far, defining meloblack in the vein of something like Mare Cognitum or Houle. Decidedly less maritime (in title or sound) and with a much more space-faring vibe going on, Apolaustic’s ability to write dynamic songs with an undeniably kinetic mix of melody, technicality and songwriting chops should be no surprise to anyone who is familiar with project mastermind Romain Negro’s previous membership of excellent progressive/medloic/technical death metal band Stortregn.Indeed, comparing No Plenitude Without Suffering to Stortregn’s younger black metal sibling would not be entirely inappropriate, as it exhibits the same mix of soul, shred and sheer scope, if so far lacking absolute supernova’s like "Grand Nexion Abyss” or “Xeno Chaos”.For any enjoyers of melodic black metal of quality and pedigree unfuckwithable, look no further. But please do actually, there’s three more entries. No Plenitude Without Suffering by APOLAUSTIC 3. Hellripper - CoronachAs it stomps, gallops and jigs between fun, fury and a finisher of true grandeur, since I last covered it in April’s KK Helripper’s Coronach has proven both it’s endlessly engaging vibrancy, and its ability to engage so many of the things that can make a metal album great, but rarely show up on the same album. It’s fun, it’s solemn and majestic, it's catchy, it’s angry, it brims with energy and sounds like it’s about to rip out of its restraints, but never gets speed metal sloppy. Incredibly varied yet uniformly great, Coronach should show up in quite a few lists come year’s end, and not just the blackened ones.  Coronach (24-bit HD audio) by Hellripper 2. The Silver - Looking Glass Hymnal BlueI honestly have no idea if this is even black metal, which is also the only reason it’s not on number one. The Silver’s sophomore amalgamation of metal styles is the kind of breath-taking bricolage that makes me want to rip up my clothes and howl at the moon. Rooted in a deep romanticism, indulgent, baroque, gothic and maximalist yet never tasteless, this album embodies what I love in my heavy music while eschewing everything I don’t.Considering its members comprise veterans of Horrendous (recognize those eardrum-flayingly awesome shrieks yet?) and Crypt Sermon, the quality is perhaps not as surprising, but while neither of those other projects fully mesh with my preferences, this one really, really does.The only criticism I would level at it is that “Tow Candles” and “My Lone Dark Lantern” are simply so good that they threaten to cast shadows as dark as their lights are bright, and thus obscure their surrounding companions.  Looking Glass Hymnal Blue by The Silver 1. Miserere Luminis - SideraBut of course, my pride as a genre stickler could not survive placing anything at number oen that is not unequivocally BLACK METAL.Luckily, there is nothing disingenuous about this placement. Miserere Luminis, another stellar band out of Quebec (seriously, what’s the secret??) gracefully take the year’s twisted yet mesmerisingly beautiful throne. With an ear for blackened melodic rapture akin to Houle, riffs as snaky and entrancing as late-stage Ulcerate and the soul-rending cathartic qualities of Selbst,Sidera goes above and beyond its influences, featuring truly engrossing compositions replete with strings and probably my favorite drumming of the year so far. Gorgeous, sad and fragile without losing the razor-sharp bite that atmospheric black metal so often lacks, I have no doubt this tour-de-force will remain at or near the top come final list season, and stay in rotation far beyond the year’s end. Sidera by Miserere Luminis

items.body: German electronic duo Heldautomat released the single “Anders Sein” on August 14, 2026 via Town & Towers Records. The track is a new interpretation of “Anders Sein,” originally released by Second Decay in 1994 on the album “Taste.” The release includes a classic 12-inch mix as a digital B-side. Heldautomat is Christian Purwien (vocals and lyrics) and Thomas Kowa (synthesizers and songs). Purwien co-founded Second Decay with Andreas Sippel in 1987, and “Anders Sein” appeared on Second Decay’s 1994 album “Taste” alongside “I Hate Berlin” and “Hinter Glas.” The new Heldautomat version is built around analogue synthesizers, piano and minimalist drum-machine rhythms, keeping the melody of the original while giving the arrangement more space. “Anders Sein” follows Heldautomat’s debut single, “Am ersten Tag,” released in May 2026. The duo’s debut album, “Zwischen den Lichtern,” is scheduled for autumn 2026 and will include eleven tracks sung in German and English. “Anders Sein” is available to stream and purchase via all platforms and on Bandcamp. About Heldautomat Heldautomat is a German electronic duo formed by Christian Purwien and Thomas Kowa. Purwien began his recording career in 1987 as co-founder and vocalist of Second Decay, a project originally named Blue Velvet, alongside Andreas Sippel. Working exclusively with analogue synthesizers, Second Decay released the tape “Monochromes” in 1988, the 12-inch “Killing Desire” in 1989, the CD “La Décadence Électronique” in 1992, the maxi-CD “Hinter Glas” in 1993 and the album “Taste” in 1994, the release that introduced “Anders Sein.” Second Decay’s second album, “The Hunt,” originally released in 1996, was reissued by Emmobiz Records as a green double LP with bonus tracks in November 2025, and a second vinyl edition of “Taste” followed via Emmo.Biz Records in 2026. Thomas Kowa is a music producer, synthesizer player and thriller author whose Erik Lindberg crime series is available in audiobook form; he has previously worked with No Comment and Nine Seconds. Purwien and Kowa first collaborated as Purwien & Kowa, releasing five albums together, including “Zwei,” the three-part “Drei” series and “Vier.” In February 2026, Purwien & Kowa performed at the 18th Elektrisch Festival in Zwickau. Heldautomat, launched in 2026 with the single “Am ersten Tag,” is described by the duo as a darker and more uncompromising direction than their earlier collaborative work, built around analogue synthesizers, piano and minimalist drum-machine rhythms. “Anders Sein” is the project’s second single, revisiting a track from Purwien’s own back catalogue ahead of the debut Heldautomat album “Zwischen den Lichtern,” due in autumn 2026.
items._cn_summary: 德国电子组合 Heldautomat 发行单曲《Anders Sein》，这首作品是对 Christian Purwien 早年参与乐队 Second Decay 1994 年专辑《Taste》中同名曲目的重新演绎。新版本以模拟合成器、钢琴与极简鼓机节奏为骨架，保留了原曲旋律但让编曲留出更多空间。整体方向延续了 Second Decay 时期模拟合成器驱动的暗潮冷波路线，被组合自身描述为比此前合作更黑暗、更不妥协的方向。该单曲为其即将于秋季发行的首张专辑《Zwischen den Lichtern》的预热，专辑将收录十一首德语与英语曲目。文章本质为推广性新闻稿，缺乏独立评论视角与音乐分析。

items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

Vanishment
(Review)

Genuine Negro Jig
(Review)

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. Further reading: The Young'uns - Tiny Notes (Review) Ben Nicholls - Duets

items._cn_summary: 这是一张以1819年曼彻斯特彼得洛大屠杀为题材的概念专辑，由Young 'Uns乐队的Sean Cooney创作。专辑以原创歌曲结合历史文献、政治漫画与插画，呈现为多媒体书籍形式。音乐风格偏向英格兰传统民谣与兰开夏工业叙事歌谣，Eliza Carthy的小提琴、Sam Carter的吉他与Jennifer Reid的兰开夏工业民谣演唱共同构建了质朴的声景。歌词聚焦于普通人的小故事，捕捉集会现场的期待、骑兵冲锋时的惊恐与事后悲恸。制作上小编制但声量充沛，三位歌手的情感表达真挚有力。在当下全球范围内抗议活动遭受打压的背景下，专辑具有现实回响意义。然而从音乐本身来看，属于较为传统的人物叙事民谣范畴，在声音设计与实验性层面探索有限，对追求前卫或实验声响的听众而言创新空间不足。

items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items._cn_summary: 该专辑记录了Dr. John（Mac Rebennack Jr.）1999年在德国洛雷莱露天剧场的现场演出。演出以新奥尔良传统为底色，混合Mardi Gras庆典元素与个人经典曲目，包括NOLA经典"Iko Iko"、自创的"Right Place, Wrong Time"以及致敬Duke Ellington的"I'm Gonna Go Fishin'"。乐手阵容紧凑，Bobby Broom吉他、David Barard贝斯、Herman Ernest鼓构成四人核心。乐评文字末尾似有截断，但已传达出这是一次面向新老乐迷的档案性现场合集，以传承新奥尔良音乐遗产为主要诉求，未见明显的实验性突破或跨领域融合尝试。

Editor's note:
When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
items._genre: field recording / spoken word / documentary / sound art
items._cn_summary: 这不是传统意义上的音乐作品，而是一份田野录音与口述证词的声音档案。录音师伊恩·布伦南在芝加哥南区枪支暴力幸存者的社区中进行实地录制，参与者年龄从十七岁到六十七岁不等，许多人即兴加入讲述。作品没有任何后期配乐添加，所有声音均来自现场环境，包括街巷、机场降落航道下的噪音以及蚊子等。录制发生在一个九十四岁老人祖母家的前廊，地点与特朗普下令国民警卫队进驻同一天。专辑呈现了枪支暴力对社区的深远影响，参与者中有刚刚参加完追悼会的女性，也有失去两个儿子的长者。这份录音超越了乐评范畴，更接近社会纪实与声音艺术的交汇点，收益将捐赠给反暴力公益机构。

items.body: Dead Can Dance released the album “Anastasis” on 13 August 2012 through PIAS Recordings. The eighth studio album by the British-Australian duo Brendan Perry and Lisa Gerrard turns 14 this year. It was their first studio release in 16 years, following 1996’s “Spiritchaser,” and their first album not released on 4AD. Dead Can Dance separated in 1998 while working on a follow-up to “Spiritchaser,” cancelling the album and an accompanying tour. The duo reunited in 2005 for a 31-date world tour that did not produce new studio material. Perry announced in May 2011 that the band would record a new album and return to touring. “Anastasis” and a full world tour were confirmed together in 2012, with the tour opening in Canada days ahead of the album’s release and running into July 2013. “Anastasis” contains eight tracks: “Children of the Sun,” “Anabasis,” “Agape,” “Amnesia,” “Kiko,” “Opium,” “Return of the She-King” and “All in Good Time,” with a total running time of 56 minutes. Dead Can Dance wrote, performed and produced the album themselves; Aidan Foley handled mastering. The title is the Greek word for resurrection. “Anastasis” reached number 8 on the UK Albums Chart and number 9 on the US Billboard World Albums chart, and was certified double gold by the Independent Music Companies Association in 2014 for sales of at least 150,000 copies across Europe. Anastasis by Dead Can Dance About Dead Can Dance Dead Can Dance formed in Melbourne, Australia, in 1981 as a trio of Brendan Perry, Paul Erikson and Simon Monroe, with Lisa Gerrard joining shortly after on vocals and percussion. The band relocated to London in 1982 and signed to 4AD, releasing its self-titled debut album on 27 February 1984. Six further studio albums followed on 4AD through the 1980s and 1990s: “Spleen and Ideal” (1985), “Within the Realm of a Dying Sun” (1987), “The Serpent’s Egg” (1988), “Aion” (1990), “Into the Labyrinth” (1993) and “Spiritchaser” (1996). Perry and Gerrard disbanded the project in 1998 during sessions for a planned follow-up to “Spiritchaser,” which was never completed under that title. A reunion tour followed in 2005, taking in 31 shows across Europe and North America, including performances at the Hollywood Bowl and Radio City Music Hall backed by 40-piece orchestras. In May 2011, Perry announced through his official channels that Dead Can Dance would record new material and tour again. That work led to “Anastasis,” released via PIAS Recordings on 13 August 2012 as the band’s first album away from 4AD. Dead Can Dance followed it with “Dionysus” on PIAS Recordings in 2018, its most recent studio album to date.

items.body:
Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.
Berceuse
Tiny Sun will perform the entire album at Toronto�s Koerner Hall on May 14, 2026.

items.body: Alina Ibragimova and Cédric Tiberghien have returned to Beethoven‘s violin sonatas, this time performing exclusively on period instruments. Having previously recorded the complete cycle on modern instruments for the Wigmore Hall Live label, the duo opens this new project with the three Op. 12 sonatas and the Spring Sonata (No. 5). Ibragimova plays a c. 1775 Anselmo Bellosio violin, while Tiberghien performs on a Paul McNulty fortepiano modeled after a 1794 Anton Walter instrument. Walter was a premier maker whose fortepianos were favored by both Mozart and Beethoven, making this an ideal historical match for the repertoire. Violin Sonatas Vol. 1 Amazon Presto Apple In the Violin Sonata No. 1 in D Major, Op. 12 No. 1, the duo immediately establishes a standard of precision. The Allegro con brio is immaculate in its synchronicity and articulation, from the neatly truncated phrasing of the opening bars to the clarity of the rolling arpeggios. Despite this exacting attention to detail, the quintessential Beethovenian spirit of contrast and surprise remains fully intact; the musicians grasp the raw vitality of one moment and juxtapose it with grace and lyricism in the next. While the period instruments may not possess the powerful, rounded polish of their modern counterparts, their rawness imparts a distinct and memorable flavor. The slightly rough-around-the-edges timbre and scrappy enthusiasm only heighten the sense of authenticity in the performance. The middle movement, a theme and variations, is arguably the most emotionally eclectic section of the sonata, and the duo wastes no time exploring the character of each variation. The theme evokes the charm of a Mozart minuet, giving way to a graceful dialogue between violin and piano in the subsequent variations. As the music gathers momentum, the violin assumes an increasingly pleading tone that heightens the tension. The minor variation at the 3’48” mark is where true Beethovenian drama makes its entrance. Tiberghien and Ibragimova wholeheartedly embrace the stormy intensity, with the fortepiano providing a convincing rumble in its bass register. Of the other two sonatas in the Op. 12 set, No. 3 in E-flat Major calls to mind the Eroica symphony, not just due to the shared key, but also in its regal character. Here, the duo taps into another dimension of their artistry: the ability to create a convincing orchestral profile. The Allegro con spirito presents a noble and stately personality, while the Rondo adds a more assertive, rhythmic drive. The relative lightness of the period instruments in no way inhibits the players from generating a resplendent, full-bodied tone. The Sonata No. 2 in A Major follows and serves as the most playful, yet virtuosic, offering on the program. In the Allegro vivace, the duo brings humor and persistence to the inquisitive two-note phrases, but it is the meticulous, effortless-sounding passagework that truly stands out. This whimsical energy establishes a striking contrast with the middle movement, the only one on the album set in a minor key. Tiberghien and Ibragimova seize this rare moment of melancholy to deliver a tender, sensitive reading of real gravity. Cédric Tiberghien and Alina Ibragimova. For the Spring Sonata, the duo makes the most of the qualities of their period instruments to present a zesty, energized interpretation. A side-by-side comparison with their previous modern-instrument recording reveals pointed differences. While certain interpretive mannerisms remain — such as Tiberghien’s rubato in the piano part or Ibragimova’s crisp bowing and tight rhythms — the modern version feels warmer, mellower, and heavier, largely due to the modern piano’s resonance. Conversely, the period recording feels perfectly fitted to the idyllic, refreshing spirit of the sonata. Throughout the Allegro assai, Tiberghien displays fine control over phrase contouring. The tone of a fortepiano can often feel fleeting, yet he manages to create grounded, distinct closures to his phrases, alongside finely graded softer dynamics. Ibragimova matches this level of musicianship, offering a wide range of timbral characters. Her violin can drop to barely a whisper, yet quickly pivot to a much more adamant profile during robust passages. A minor gripe is that the violin occasionally overpowers the piano, though this may be more a matter of microphone placement than musical balance. The slow movement provides a glimpse into the opposite end of the emotional spectrum, replacing bubbling energy with a deeply satisfying calm. Once again, the period instruments lend an added angle of translucence and fragility rarely heard on modern recordings. The duo is superbly matched here, with Ibragimova providing a supportive, sensitive backdrop during the piano’s melodic lines. Richard Wigmore’s accompanying liner notes offer helpful stylistic analysis and commentary on the sonatas’ connections to other works in Beethoven’s catalogue. Ultimately, Tiberghien and Ibragimova prove fully at home in the period-instrument domain, delivering performances of real dimension and personality. Should you buy this album if you already own the previous cycle by the duo? The answer is yes, and certainly if you are looking for what promises to be a first-class period-instrument cycle of Beethoven’s complete violin sonatas. 1961年生まれ、兵庫県神戸市出身。1986年渡仏。パリ第8大学でベアトリス・ディディエ、パリ国立高等音楽院=高等師範=トゥール大学合同音楽学課程でデイヴィッド・チャ... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る ペルトコスキ＆トゥールーズ・キャピトル国立管 日本ツアーへ発つ直前の舞台 2025／26シーズン末のフィルハーモニー・ド・パリには、フィンランドの優れた教授ヨルマ・パヌラ門下の若手二人があいついで指揮台に立った。 26歳のタルモ・ペルトコスキは2024年からトゥールーズ・キャピトル国立管弦楽団の音楽監督を務めている。本拠地トゥールーズの演奏に続いたパリ公演は、成功裡に終わった日本ツアーへ出発する直前の6月2日に行われた。 前半はアレクサンドル・カントロフを迎えてのベートーヴェン「ピアノ協奏曲第4番」ト長調だった。冒頭の第1主題から、カントロフのピアノは、ソロ楽器の即興性から生まれる華やかさと、作曲家が曲に託した心情を音に込めた内省的な側面の双方を兼ね備えていた。その印象は全3楽章を通じて変わらなかったが、この二面性が実現された大きな要因はピアノ独奏を最大限に尊重した指揮にあった。 自身もピアニストであるペルトコスキは、オーケストラを常に安定したテンポに保つことにより、ソリストの自由を最大限に広げた。阿吽の呼吸によって、苛烈さと優しい抒情が鮮やかに音となって広がっていった。この間、一度としてピアニストのほうに視線を向けなかったことは、この指揮者の耳が破格であることの証左であろう。 カントロフの演奏そのものが、1台の楽器というよりもオーケストラを思わせるだけに、この組み合わせによって、ベートーヴェンがこの曲に明快に打ち出した「交響作品」という特徴が際立って感じられた。聴き手は、あたかもピアノを伴った交響的幻想曲を前にしているような気持ちにひたされた。 カントロフは現役ピアニストのなかでも傑出したテクニックの持ち主だが、テクニックがあくまでも表現のための手段となっているので、聴いていて鼻につかない。そして彼の手にかかると、曲想は常に自然に流れていく。5曲ある楽聖のピアノ協奏曲のなかで、もっともインティメートな作品が、彼の気性にいちばんピッタリしているのかもしれない。 アンコールは夢を見ているかのようなブラームス「3つの間奏曲」作品117から「第1番」変ホ長調、次いで音符が自在に飛翔するかのようなスクリャービン《焔に向かって》だった。 後半のマーラー「交響曲第6番《悲劇的》」イ短調では、第1楽章の行進曲を思わせる冒頭から、弦楽器の音量を抑えめにして、全4楽章を通じて感情を抑制した演奏となった。音色の多彩さと細部に留意した指揮によって、トゥールーズ・キャピトル国立管の華やかな管楽器群のソロが前面に出た。 前半の一部において緊迫感がやや低下した箇所があったにせよ、第3楽章アンダンテから第4楽章フィナーレにかけてのドラマの高揚感は誰にも抗しがたかった。指揮者に対する団員の信頼は絶大で、壮大な曲が終わると、観客に負けない拍手が舞台の上に湧き上がった。 パリ管がマケラ指揮、ファウストの独奏で28年ぶりにシューマン「ヴァイオリン協奏曲」 シューマン「ヴァイオリン協奏曲」が終わって、拍手に応えるイザベル・ファウスト（中央左）とクラウス・マケラ（中央右）© 三光 洋 6月10日には、パリで圧倒的な人気を誇るクラウス・マケラがパリ管弦楽団を指揮した。 シューマン「ヴァイオリン協奏曲」ニ短調は名ヴァイオリニスト、ヨーゼフ・ヨアヒムのために1853年秋に一気に書かれた。しかし、ヨアヒムが「弾くのが難しく、舞台映えしない」という理由を挙げて演奏しなかっただけでなく、総譜の出版も差し止めてしまった。作曲家は生前に耳にすることができず、初演されたのはナチス時代の1937年になってからといういわくつきの作品である。パリ管が取り上げるのも、1998年以来28年ぶりの2度目で、きわめてまれだ。 イザベル・ファウストは楽譜を見つめながら、細やかな感受性を反映したよどみのない輝きのある演奏により、高貴なシューマンの世界へと聴き手を導いてくれた。マケラの指揮も優しくソリストを包み込む繊細なものだった。 最後の「幻想序曲《ロメオとジュリエット》」は、シェイクスピア劇の数場面をチャイコフスキーが卓越したドラマ感覚により音にしている。リムスキー=コルサコフが「ロシア音楽でもっとも美しい」と絶賛した、コールアングレとヴィオラによる「愛の主題」はとくに名高い。エネルギーの横溢したマケラの指揮に鼓舞されて一体となったパリ管の奏者たちによって、二人の恋人たちの燃え上がる情念がほとばしり、華やいだシーズン閉幕となった。
